MANILA, Philippines – Rosal (Champi) weakened from a super typhoon into a typhoon on Thursday afternoon, October 22, but rainfall and wind warnings have yet to be lifted for portions of Northern Luzon.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in its 5 pm bulletin on Thursday that Rosal’s maximum sustained winds are down to 165 kilometers per hour. Its gustiness has also eased to 205 km/h.
At its peak, Rosal had maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h.

As of 4 pm on Thursday, the typhoon was located 350 kilometers east of Itbayat, Batanes, moving northwest at only 15 km/h. It will be at its closest point to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, October 23.
PAGASA said Rosal will continue to trigger heavy to intense rain in Batanes (100-200 millimeters) and moderate to heavy rain in Cagayan (50-100 mm) in the next 24 hours.

On Thursday evening, the typhoon may also bring rain with gusty winds to Ilocos Norte, Apayao, and Isabela, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Ilocos Sur, La Union, and Aurora.

Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
articles.summary: Four members of the so-called Gang Suppression Force have been missing since Sunday.

blocks.text: El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday.
Nayib Bukele wrote in a post on X that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive.
They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups.
They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti.
According to Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive.
He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping".
Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area.

A statement released by the Armed Forces of El Salvador on Sunday said the group was ambushed while travelling back to its camp in an armoured vehicle, which caught fire after being hit by explosives.
So far, no gang has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Salvadoran helicopters were deployed to assist, with multiple attempts to make an approach by land and air hampered by fighting and local security conditions, the armed forces said.
On Wednesday, before Bukele announced the launch of the military operation, the GSF said it was searching for the four missing personnel following the attack.
It added that it had "engaged armed gang elements, with helicopter support" and that early reports had indicated that several gang members were killed.

Earlier this week, the UN warned that Haiti's armed gangs were adapting to intensified security conditions, saying that they were "stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas".
Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and two weeks ago postponed presidential and legislative elections - scheduled for 13 December - indefinitely.
The country has been wracked by economic chaos, a political vacuum and increasingly violent gang warfare since its president was assassinated in 2021.
More than 5,500 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti in 2024. Armed gangs currently control about 85% of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

articles.title: DOJ says there's possible resurgence of scam hubs
articles.summary: Justice Undersecretary Nicky Ty on Thursday said there may be a resurgence of small-scale scam hub operations in the Philippines following the arrest and rescue of several individuals in various…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 6:12pm

Justice Undersecretary Nicky Ty on Thursday said there may be a resurgence of small-scale scam hub operations in the Philippines following the arrest and rescue of several individuals in various raids.
In early October, authorities rescued more than 230 scam hub workers in Zamboanga Sibugay.

“It’s possible that there is a resurgence, but nevertheless, compared to before mas maliit talaga, not just in the scale of operations but also on the composition of the foreign nationals who are rescued or found within these scam hubs,” Ty, the Undersecretary-in-Charge of IACAT, said at a press briefing.
Ty added that most of the individuals rescued before were mostly Chinese, along with some Vietnamese, Indonesian, Myanmar, Nepalese, and African.
“Ngayon, it’s really mostly Chinese ‘yung mga nahanap natin,” he said.
(Now, we’re finding that it’s really mostly Chinese.)
When asked what could be the reason for this, Ty cited the visa-free arrangement for Chinese nationals, among other reasons.

“Another reason, although nakita ito, na identify ito from the ground, na some Chinese individuals who were located in the scam hubs actually entered the Philippines using the visa-free arrangement. And some of them are actually overstaying,” he said.

(Another reason, although this was seen and identified on the ground, is that some Chinese individuals who were located in the scam hubs actually entered the Philippines using the visa-free arrangement. And some of them are actually overstaying.)
Ty said the Department of Justice (DOJ) is still collecting information.
“Hindi natin maitatanggi, ano, na ‘yang isang privilege na binigay natin sa mga Chinese tourists napagsamantalahan sa problema na ito,” he added.
(We cannot deny that this privilege we granted to Chinese tourists has been exploited in this problem.)
He said the IACAT and DOJ has yet to give its recommendation regarding the visa-free arrangement.
The Philippines retained its Tier 1 ranking in the US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Meta strikes deal with Zuckerberg to protect him from California wealth tax
articles.summary: Company says deal will keep its chief executive living in California even if state brings in one-off billionaire tax

blocks.text: Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to protect him from the threat of a California wealth tax targeting billionaires.

The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where its headquarters are located.

Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years
Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40 – a one-time 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state.

Zuckerberg, worth $239bn according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.
In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders.
This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of this new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company.

Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has dubbed Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs.

“Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay. In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week.
Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn.
But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s landmark lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings.
In a separate case, a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a trial found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
Meta also revealed it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: EU's Sakharov Prize won by the International Criminal Court
articles.summary: The EU has announced the International Criminal Court as the winner of this year's Sakharov Prize.

image.caption: The ICC was founded in 2002 in The HagueImage: Jiji Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: The International Criminal Court (ICC) has won this year's Sakharov Prize, awarded by the European Union to individuals and organizations in recognition of their work to support and protect human rights and democracy.
The decision to award the Netherlands-based court, and its officials, was announced by European Parliament President Roberta Metsola.

"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the Court in upholding international law and justice," Metsola said in the European Parliament.
In naming the ICC as the prize winner, Metsola also took time to recognize the two other finalists: Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and the Iranian twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi.
The prize ceremony will take place in December.
What is the International Criminal Court?
Set up in 2002 in the Hague, the ICC is responsible for prosecuting the most serious of crimes, including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The ICC has recently come under sanctions from the US government under President Donald Trump in response to what Washington called political bias. The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The US said it wants to "dismantle" the court.
The awarding of the Sakharov Prize is a further show of support after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
More to come...

articles.summary: The Office of the Solicitor General notes that the 12 separate opinions accompanying the Supreme Court ruling 'reflect the complexity of the constitutional questions presented and the differing…

The Office of the Solicitor General notes that the 12 separate opinions accompanying the Supreme Court ruling 'reflect the complexity of the constitutional questions presented and the differing judicial perspectives on their resolution'

items: The Office of Solicitor General will seek clarification and partial reconsideration of the Supreme Court's ruling on unprogrammed appropriations, emphasizing the need for safeguards in budgetary powers.

The Supreme Court ruled that the 2024 and 2025 budgets are unconstitutional due to Congress' increase of the national government's proposed budget through unprogrammed appropriations, which must comply with specific conditions.

Budget Secretary Kim De Leon stated that the Department of Budget and Management is coordinating with the OSG to address potential issues arising from the ruling, while the Supreme Court clarified that previously spent funds do not need to be returned.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of Solicitor General (OSG) said on Thursday, October 22, that it will seek clarification and partial reconsideration of the recent Supreme Court’s ruling on unprogrammed appropriations (UAs).

“With utmost respect to the Court, the OSG will seek clarification and partial reconsideration of certain aspects of the Decision, particularly the guardrails prescribed for the exercise of budgetary powers,” the OSG said in a statement.

“The OSG agrees that safeguards are essential to ensure transparency, accountability, and fiscal discipline in the use of public funds. The complex challenge, however, lies in distinguishing the safeguards that are required by the Constitution from those whose formulation falls within the constitutionally provided powers of Congress and the Executive,” it added.
The OSG noted that the 12 separate opinions accompanying the ruling “reflect the complexity of the constitutional questions presented and the differing judicial perspectives on their resolution.”
“The OSG will carefully consider these opinions in its further action,” it said.

“The OSG remains committed to assisting the Court in ensuring that safeguards governing public expenditure are firmly anchored in the Constitution, while preserving the powers entrusted to the political branches in service of the Filipino people,” the OSG added.
In its ruling on Tuesday, October 20, the Supreme Court ruled that the 2024 and 2025 budgets are unconstitutional since Congress increased the president’s proposed national budget through UAs.
UAs are standby appropriations that may only be used once specific conditions are met, such as when government revenues exceed targets or when foreign grants and loans are on the table.
The Supreme Court did not rule that UAs are unconstitutional but clarified that UAs must be compliant with the following:

items: There should be no lump sums in unprogrammed appropriations.
The conditions for using new income and additional earnings from the government’s non-tax revenue incomes should be differentiated from programmed and unprogrammed expenditures.
Congress should have sufficient standards in terms of prioritization for spending if there is more than one purpose under unprogrammed appropriations.
The provision for the unprogrammed appropriations should be within the national fiscal program plan found in the budget and “consistent with its nature as a narrow contingent appropriation.”

blocks.text: During the budget hearing of the Department of Budget and Management in the Senate on Thursday, Budget Secretary Kim De Leon said the DBM is closely working with the OSG to seek clarification before the High Court.
De Leon said that there are a lot of issues that may arise from the recent Supreme Court ruling, like unreleased UAs, unobligated allotment, and unpaid obligations from previous years.

blocks.caption: SolgGen to seek clarification, partial reconsideration of SC ruling on unprogrammed funds

blocks.text: The High Court had clarified that there was no need to return the money that had already been spent following the doctrine of operative fact. This means completed programs whose beneficiaries acted in good faith won’t be undone.

The doctrine, however, “does not shield authors, proponents, or implementors from criminal, civil, or administrative liability unless the proper tribunals explicitly find that they acted in good faith.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Former DOH chiefs alarmed over proposed cut for health promotion in 2027
articles.summary: Under the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, the House of Representatives reduced the health promotion budget to P485 million

blocks.text: LEPTO. Leptospirosis patients are treated in the leptospirosis ward of San Lazaro Hospital in Manila on August 26, 2026.
Rappler
Under the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, the House of Representatives reduced the health promotion budget to P485 million

items: Former health secretaries have raised concerns over the significant reduction of the health promotion budget in the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, arguing it violates the Universal Health Care Law.

The House of Representatives cut the health promotion budget to P485 million from P2.5 billion, which health experts warn undermines efforts to prevent noncommunicable diseases and could lead to higher future healthcare costs.

Health officials emphasize that a severely underfunded health promotion budget will negatively impact vulnerable communities, stripping them of necessary resources to protect against preventable health risks.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Former health secretaries sounded the alarm on the drastic cut to the health promotion budget in the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB), as it supposedly violates the Universal Health Care (UHC) Law.

Under the 2027 GAB, the House of Representatives allocated P275.85 billion for the Department of Health‘s new appropriations, up from the P263.62 billion in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
But the House, in its version, reduced the health promotion budget to P485 million, from the P2.5 billion in the NEP.

On Thursday, October 22, Healthy Philippines Alliance warned that the House did not follow Section 30 of the UHC Law, which provides that “the cost of implementing health promotion programs shall be at least one percent (1%) of the DOH’s total budget appropriations.”

“A budget cut of this scale undermines the mandate of the UHC Law. It is counterproductive to our goal of achieving a financially sustainable Universal Health Care which is fundamentally guaranteed to every Filipino,” said Dr. Manuel Dayrit, a health secretary during the Arroyo administration.
Dayrit urged Congress to treat health promotion as a core investment rather than an expendable cost, as health promotion and disease prevention is the foundation of the UHC.
Rappler reached out to Nueva Ecija 1st District Representative Mika Suansing, the House appropriations chairperson, for comment. Her staff said she is already on maternity leave.
Rappler also reached out to Bataan 2nd District Representative Albert Garcia, the DOH’s budget sponsor, for comment.

“Slashing funding for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases or NCDs will ultimately cost the government far more in secondary care and emergency hospitalizations in the future. Diabetes, heart and kidney disease, and hypertension are overwhelming Filipino families and draining our healthcare system,” said Dr. Jaime Galvez Tan, lead convenor of Healthy Philippines Alliance and health secretary during the Ramos administration.
Dr. Esperanza Cabral, another health chief during the Arroyo administration, said the government cannot protect vulnerable communities in a “severely underfunded” health promotion budget.

“When the budget for health promotion shrinks to P400 million, Filipino families, especially those from low-income households, lose the support and resources they need to protect them from preventable risks. It strips the poor of their right to services that can save their lives,” she said.
The House’s budget amendments review subcommittee proposed budget realignments for the DOH amounting to P28.36 billion.
Of the amount, P25 billion was added to the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) program, which civil society groups have described as “soft pork.”

blocks.caption: Health groups to lawmakers: Increase PhilHealth budget, not MAIFIP funding

blocks.text: Other DOH programs with higher funding figures were the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, nationally procured commodities for prevention and control of communicable disease, and operations of DOH regional hospitals.

The Senate is still deliberating the 2027 budget proposal. A bicameral conference committee will be convened if there are differences in the versions of the House and Senate, before the proposed spending plan is brought to the President. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump’s war and tariffs have battered Alaska. A pro-oil Democrat could flip the key Senate seat
articles.summary:
Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the state

Mary Peltola’s campaign to represent

blocks.text: Mary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the massive state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.

She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. Along the Arctic Ocean, she’s heard of communities where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights.
“Nobody can afford that,” Peltola said in an interview.

Alaska, a right-leaning state that’s about twice the size of Texas but the third least-populous in the country, has always been among the more expensive places to live, and the price increases in the state’s rural areas haven’t necessarily been felt to the same degree in the more populous cities and towns.

Yet the state’s Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the 3 November midterms. The Senate seat currently held by two-term Republican Dan Sullivan is a top prize.

“In 23 short days, we’re going to be voting both [Republican congressman] Nick Begich and Dan Sullivan out of office, and they richly deserve it,” the chair of the state Democratic party, Eric Croft, said at a press conference last week.
“They are self-serving, self-dealing DC politicians who repeatedly voted to make life harder and more expensive for Alaskans.”

blocks.caption: The Republican US senator Dan Sullivan after a debate with Mary Peltola in Anchorage, Alaska, on 15 October 2026. Photograph: Kerry Tasker/Reuters

blocks.text: All signs indicate that Republicans are taking seriously the threat posed by Peltola, an Alaska native and former US House lawmaker who supports oil and gas and gun rights. Outside groups have poured in tens of millions of dollars into supporting both candidates, and last week Donald Trump made the long journey from Washington DC to the conservative Matanuska-Susitna valley to rally voters behind Sullivan, who has trailed in some recent polls.

“Here in Alaska, the Democrats are running radical left Mary Peltola for the Senate. If she gets in, you’re screwed,” the president told a packed sports center in Wasilla, which is best known outside the state as being the home town of Sarah Palin, the Republican former vice-presidential nominee.

On the campaign trail, Peltola and Sullivan have dueled over who would do a better job lowering costs for Alaskans, and also representing its vital fishing and oil and gas industries in the US Capitol. There have been mutual accusations of allegiances not to a state known as “the last frontier” but to special interests in the Lower 48, while Sullivan has accused Peltola of denigrating Alaskans after a report that she mistreated her staffers.

The incumbent has his own unique vulnerability in the form of a similarly named Republican challenger who made it through the state’s top-four primary, and could split his support. And while polls open on 3 November, the outcome may not be known for days – Alaska has always taken a long time to count its ballots, and its use of ranked-choice voting in the Senate contest could result in an even lengthier wait for the final result.
No state like it

Since becoming the 49th state in 1959, Alaska has only once supported a Democratic candidate in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson in 1964. But its politics are nuanced – bipartisan majorities currently control the legislature and the frontrunner in the governor’s race is a Democrat. In the race for the state’s lone US House seat, the party has coalesced behind the independent candidate Bill Hill to take on Begich.

“Sixty per cent of Alaskans do not identify with the Republican or the Democratic party. We are a great example in this state of how government should work,” Hill, who is receiving support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in an interview.

A former state lawmaker, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022 when she won a special election to replace Don Young, the long-serving Republican congressman who died at 88, and became the first Alaska native in Congress. She was elected to a full term later that year, then lost re-election to Begich in 2024. This year, Peltola is viewed as the best candidate Democrats could field to take on Sullivan.

blocks.caption: A fish hatchery in Valdez, Alaska, on 23 August 2023. Peltola centers her campaign on the slogan “fish, family, freedom”. Photograph: Michael Siluk/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

blocks.text: Centering her campaign on the slogan “fish, family, freedom”, she has added an Alaskan twist to the cost-focused platform many Democrats have adopted nationwide. Visitors to her campaign website can play a video game intended to highlight her views on bycatch, or the accidental netting of other species by trawlers, which has become a major controversy in Alaska as salmon runs have dwindled.

Peltola opposes Trump’s tariff regime, noting it has driven up costs for imports from Canada, which separates Alaska from the rest of the country. She has also condemned his decision to attack Iran and spark a conflict that has driven costs for gasoline and diesel – which typically arrive by barge or ship in the state’s interior and island communities – even higher than usual.

“These really frivolous decisions are just putting Alaskans in a bind, and we’re really paying the price for these weird partisan wars,” Peltola said as she visited a picket line of flight attendants at Anchorage’s main airport. With a laugh, she added: “I don’t know what’s funny about that, but it’s funny.”
after newsletter promotion

Sullivan, her opponent, was first elected in 2014 after ousting a Democratic incumbent. He serves alongside Republican Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s senior senator who is one of the most outspoken Trump critics in the Senate, but has nonetheless remained a firm ally of of the president, even as his popularity has waned, unlike many vulnerable Republicans who have sought distance. Sullivan has emphasized his advocacy for Alaska’s military installations, as well as the state’s long list of proposed oil developments and major infrastructure projects that he argues will only come to fruition if Republicans are kept in charge.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators march during the No Kings protest in downtown Anchorage on 28 March 2026. Photograph: Hasan Akbas/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Joe Biden, Schumer, their Democratic allies came after Alaska with a barrage of executive orders to shut down our state, kill jobs, drive up the cost of energy, and my opponent, Mary Peltola, not only did nothing to stop it, she enabled it,” Sullivan said as he rallied with Trump.

“They try to kill our jobs and turn us into a national park. Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs.”

He gained new ammunition against Peltola in September, when the New York Times reported allegations that she had verbally and physically abused her staff and used slurs. “My opponent really doesn’t like her fellow Alaskans. She just doesn’t,” Sullivan told supporters in Wasilla.

Peltola’s campaign has said parts of the report are not true, and noted some of the behavior occurred when she was grieving the death of her husband in a plane crash, and the death of her mother around the same time. When Peltola was asked about the report during a debate with Sullivan last week, she replied: “I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications.”
‘Priced out of petroleum’

Alaska is one of the nation’s top oil-producing states, and every year its permanent fund pays each resident a dividend that’s usually upwards of $1,000. But production, which is concentrated on the state’s North Slope, has steadily declined since peaking in the late 1980s, and how to manage the resource is a constant topic in the state’s politics.

blocks.caption: A caribou on the tundra near the Trans Alaska pipeline system on 9 May 2025 near the Atigun pass in Alaska. Photograph: Lance King/Getty Images

blocks.text: Sullivan is all-in on oil production, supporting moves by Trump to open up more protected federal land and waters to drilling, which could offer new revenue opportunities. He cheered the president’s announcement that South Korea would invest $54bn to build a long-discussed natural gas pipeline across the state, although reports have since emerged that Seoul has agreed to no such deal.

Though she was in the House of Representatives for just over two years, Peltola has taken credit for pushing Joe Biden to approve the massive Willow oil project, over the objections of environmentalists. But she also emphasizes the opportunities renewable energy could present to Alaska’s communities, and is cognizant that she is a member of a party that prioritizes fighting the climate crisis, which many believe requires curbing oil and gas production.
“We do need more oil production in our state for our state revenues to pay for our schools, our roads, our public safety,” Peltola said.
But the sky-high prices for gas in parts of Alaska are proof to the candidate that oil is not the solution alone.
“When you’re paying $26 a gallon for gas or diesel, we’re priced out of petroleum,” she said.

articles.title: Experts alarmed by ‘less transparent’ CDC as US measles deaths rise
articles.summary:
Agency declines to reveal in which state latest measles death occurred as it delays reporting other measles deaths

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added a third…

blocks.text: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added a third measles death to its dashboard on Wednesday, but the agency would not reveal whether the death occurred in Pennsylvania or another state – which is “notable” as the agency delays reporting other measles deaths, experts say.

The CDC cited privacy laws in not sharing the name of the state, but experts say there are no privacy concerns in doing so – and this information is important for the public to have as the outbreak continues accelerating, growing by 8% in one week to 4,410 confirmed cases so far this year, nearly double last year’s count.

“Due to privacy laws and legal restrictions, NCHS [the National Center for Health Statistics] cannot identify a state or provide additional details about the third individual,” a spokesperson with the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told the Guardian in response to questions about where the death took place.
The spokesperson did not respond to follow-up questions about which laws and restrictions prevented that information from being shared.

“I don’t buy it,” said Dorit Reiss, a professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. “Naming a state won’t be giving personal details, and they give the number of cases in each state,” she said, adding there was “nothing to prevent giving numbers of deaths in each”.

The CDC is not governed by Hipaa as health providers are. The agency is instead guided by the Federal Privacy Act, which usually prohibits disclosing government records about specific individuals, said Lindsay Wiley, professor of law and faculty director of the Health Law and Policy Program at UCLA Law.

“But this general prohibition only applies to information that reveals an individual’s identity,” Wiley said. “It’s hard to see how identifying the state where a death occurred would allow the public to identify the patient.”

At the same time, it’s “not unheard of” for agencies to use an “overly broad, unwarranted interpretation of privacy protections to decline to share information that they prefer not to share anyway, because it may be seen as damaging to their reputation or agenda”, Wiley said.

The CDC switched in September to using NCHS rather than the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), a system that usually reports deaths quickly and provides the state where a death occurs. The agency has not given a clear reason for the change.
When only a few deaths have occurred, NCHS usually does not say where those deaths are happening, which is one of the weaknesses in using it to report information like this.

“But it’s also in the news, so it already is likely identifiable,” said Debra Houry, former chief medical officer at the CDC. And the agency still has access to other reporting systems, like NNDSS, to know which state has deaths, Houry said.
Pennsylvania has strict privacy laws about not reporting demographic information or medical details, but “that still wouldn’t limit state and deaths”, she said.

Pennsylvania has now reported a total of six deaths, with the most recent case still under investigation by state officials. By carefully tracing the cause of death before reporting it on the state dashboard, officials in Pennsylvania are “doing the right thing”, Houry said.

The CDC dashboard only lists three deaths from measles this year, despite five confirmed deaths in Pennsylvania. The agency has not given a reason for the delay; usually, the NCHS system is updated within days of states sending information.
Reiss said it was “a change from past practice, and not a good one. [The] CDC is being less transparent than in the past.”

Not having a clear picture of what’s happening in each state, including a possible death from measles, makes it hard to understand risk levels, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “You’d like to know what the activity is in your state.”

Offit said he wondered if the secrecy was “coming from the top”, since officials such as Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, or Erica Schwartz, CDC director, have reportedly given orders to decrease the measles death count.

It’s also not clear if the public is receiving accurate numbers of cases, Offit said. A 39-year-old woman in Franklin county, Pennsylvania, died of an acute cardiac event, a known but very rare complication of measles infection, Offit pointed out.
“When you see something like that, you’re looking at the tip of a much bigger iceberg,” he said. “Are you really monitoring how many adults are getting infected? I doubt it.”
It’s also harder to reach adults who may be at risk because they’re not vaccinated, because most vaccination requirements happen at the school level, Offit said. “What do you do for adults?”

The decision not to include all deaths from measles is “notable” and will likely have wide-ranging consequences, Offit said. The CDC has offered to send a support team to help Pennsylvania with the outbreak, but state and local officials may be wary of working alongside staff at an agency that is refusing to record accurate data, Offit said. “You wonder, ‘Can you trust them?’ It’s really that bad.”

articles.title: In reliably blue Minnesota, could Democrats do the unthinkable and lose a Senate seat?
articles.summary:
Frustration with a sprawling fraud scandal has cut Peggy Flanagan’s poll lead – could ex-NFL reporter Michele Tafoya win a first statewide election for Republicans in 20 years?

As Democrats…

blocks.text: As Democrats fight to regain control of the US Senate, hopes are rising in states – from Kansas to Texas – where they have not prevailed in decades. But in Minnesota, where Republicans have not won statewide election since 2006, the contest for an open Senate seat is closer than expected.

Should Peggy Flanagan – the state’s Democratic lieutenant governor – win the election, she will be the first Native American woman to serve in the US Senate. But history has not yet been made. The closely watched Cook Political Report shifted its rating on the race this week from “likely Democrat” to “lean Democrat”.

Flanagan has made hundreds of stops throughout Minnesota this year, first in a contested primary where she beat out a more moderate congresswoman, and now as she faces Republican challenger Michele Tafoya.

Tafoya, a more pragmatic choice for Minnesota Republicans than in previous US Senate elections, has sought to cast herself as a pro-choice Republican, though she has not spelled out what her stance is on access to abortion. She has also broken rank with the Trump administration on the Iran war after previously supporting it.
Unlike some Republicans who have sought Trump’s support,Tafoya didn’t rush to embrace the president’s recent endorsement. “I heard about that,” she said.

blocks.caption: Michele Tafoya speaks on Minnesota Public Radio last week. Photograph: Kerem Yücel/Minnesota Public Radio/AP

blocks.text: Most polls have shown Flanagan ahead – but not with a large lead, and lagging behind those built by Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic US senator now running for governor, in polls against her challenger, Minnesota house speaker Lisa Demuth. The most recent poll by the Minnesota Star Tribune earlier this month showed Flanagan up four points.

Flanagan’s central liability comes from her current job. As the lieutenant governor in Tim Walz’s administration, she is tied into a sprawling fraud problem in the state’s social services. Without an incumbent on the ballot for governor or US Senate, some voters may take out their frustration on Flanagan.
Walz decided not to seek a third term as governor, after initially saying he would, because of the fraud issue and the political response to it.

Republicans have not won a statewide race in Minnesota in 20 years. “There is a path. It’s not a wide path, but there is a path for Republicans,” said Blois Olson, an independent political analyst in Minnesota.

While Minnesota Democrats have dominated statewide races the past two decades, the state is not deeply blue: the state legislature is now split, with the house tied and Democrats controlling the senate. Some see Flanagan, a progressive who supports the proposed Medicare for All model of universal healthcare, as farther left than the statewide electorate.
“It sets up a race where Republicans are as optimistic as anything,” Olson said. “But until Republicans win statewide, you can’t think they’re going to win. It’s kind of like Democrats in Texas.”

Trump’s approval rating among Minnesotans is at a personal low. His surge of immigration agents into the state sits heavy on the minds of many, and features in campaign ads against Republicans. Two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were killed by federal agents in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge earlier this year.

Trump has continued to attack the state, and its leaders, and often rails against the state’s Somali population. In the only debate for Minnesota’s US Senate seat ahead of the general election, Tafoya wouldn’t say whether she would attend if Trump staged a rally in the state.

National Republicans have so far not swooped in to boost Tafoya – a signal that the race is not a top priority, or that their money is more needed to defend their seats in unexpected places, including Kansas.

Flanagan, at a union press conference earlier this month, said she always runs for office as though she’s 10 points behind, including when she ran unopposed for the state legislature, when she still knocked doors most nights. In the primary, she noted, polls showed a close race between her and Craig, but Flanagan won by nearly 20 percentage points.

“I’ve always been underestimated, and that’s OK. That just means I work a little bit harder,” she said. “And frankly, there are more people in the state of Minnesota who understand that they are being squeezed, and when the response to that pain from my opponent is to say that people should take one less trip to Starbucks and keep a stiff upper lip, that is a slap in the face to working people all across Minnesota.”
Tafoya did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.

Signs for Tafoya dot the yards of the Twin Cities suburbs. Olson, the analyst, said he heard from people who knock on doors to talk to voters that the conversations at people’s doors in swing districts after the primary changed.

“I have somebody to vote for, and it’s not Mike Lindell,” he said, explaining how some Republicans felt about the pillow salesman and election denier who lost the party’s gubernatorial primary. Lindell had been endorsed by Trump.
Voters are getting hit with ads on social media from Flanagan, too, who talks about the competitiveness of the race and offers up her wild rice hotdish recipe to anyone who donates to her campaign.

Tafoya, 61, made her career as a sports broadcaster, and worked for NBC as a sideline reporter covering the NFL. After she left that job, shebecame a political commentator. She has never run for, or held, elected office.

Flanagan, 47, has, by contrast, spent her career in politics – first as an organizer and then working her way up in elected offices, from school board to state legislature and then to lieutenant governorship.

blocks.caption: Peggy Flanagan says she runs for office as though she’s 10 points behind. Photograph: Kerem Yücel/Minnesota Public Radio/AP

blocks.text: Tina Smith, the Democrat who now holds the US Senate seat, decided not to seek re-election this year, saying she wanted to retire and spend time with her grandchildren. Smith endorsed Flanagan in the primary and has campaigned with her.

Tafoya, needing independent and centrist votes to win in a left-leaning state, calls herself a pro-choice conservative. In her prior public comments on abortion, she has said she supports bans on abortion after 12 or 15 weeks.
During the debate, hosted by Minnesota Public Radio last week, she could not explain what her position entailed. “Reasonable access is reasonable access,” she said.

Republicans in Minnesota need the anti-abortion community’s votes, as well as those of gun rights advocates and diehard Trump supporters, said Michael Brodkorb, a commentator and former deputy chair of the Republican party of Minnesota. Some, including a prominent pastor, have said they will not vote for Tafoya because of her approval of abortion to any degree. A write-in candidate is running for the seat in large part because she wanted voters to have an anti-abortion option on the ballot.
In her most recent ad, Tafoya says she’ll stand up to Trump if she needs to. “If she had delivered that message from the beginning, then it would be more credible,” Brodkorb said.

On fraud, Flanagan has said she believes fraud of any kind is unacceptable and supports harsher penalties and an independent inspector general. But, she has said throughout her campaign, Walz has said the buck stops with him on fraud.

One of the central questions for voters lies in someone who isn’t on the ballot: Trump, and whether the state’s next senator would provide a check on presidential power. Flanagan has said Tafoya would be a rubber stamp for the president, citing her opponent’s previous reluctance to publicly differ from Trump’s positions. Tafoya has said she would be an “equal-opportunity pain in the ass to any corrupt career politician”.

“You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who is a very respected person,” Trump said when he recently endorsed Tafoya. “It’s hard to win because they cheat on their elections too, you know I thought I won Minnesota three times.”
Trump lost Minnesota three times. Minnesota has not voted for a Republican president since 1972.
As soon as Trump endorsed Tafoya, Flanagan put up a campaign ad highlighting the endorsement, his stamp of approval a likely negative for a swath of Minnesota voters.

blocks.text: At a time when standards for choices of elective officials seem to be on the decline, many still look to the SC as a stronghold of justice and fairness to which high standards still apply. Has it lived up to those expectations?

items: The Judicial and Bar Council began public interviews for candidates to replace retiring Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, with five Supreme Court justices vying for the position.
Incumbent President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will make his second and third Supreme Court appointments, following the upcoming retirements of Gesmundo and Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier.
Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa are the candidates interviewed on October 22.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
On Thursday, October 22, the Judicial and Bar Council began public interviews for those vying for the post that will be vacated by Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who is retiring on November 6.
His replacement will be the country’s 28th chief justice (CJ) in a court still packed with Rodrigo Duterte appointees. At present, 12 justices out of 15 were appointed by the former president.
You might want to read stories related to the CJ appointment.

items: 5 Supreme Court justices vie to become next chief justice
Appellate court justices, SolGen among candidates for next SC justice

blocks.text: Incumbent President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s next choices for the Supreme Court (SC) will be his second and third, respectively — replacements for Gesmundo and Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier, who will retire on November 16. If you recall, Marcos’ first appointee was Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025.
Justice reporter Jairo Bolledo profiles the candidates competing to replace Javier in this first of a two-part report.

Scheduled for CJ interviews on Thursday are Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, appointed to the High Court in 2012 at age 49, and Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa, appointed in 2016 when he was 56. Both were hand-picked by former president Benigno Aquino III.

Thus far, Leonen is the second youngest justice to be appointed to the SC after Justice Manuel Moran, who joined the High Bench at age 45. Leonen had served as government’s chief peace negotiator with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, carved a name for himself in the field of human rights, was dean of the UP College of Law, and had even weathered an impeachment complaint in 2021.

Critics, however, remember the Leonen-penned unanimous SC decision, which said in 2025 that the impeachment complaint against Vice President Sara Duterte was unconstitutional owing to a redefinition of the one-year bar rule and violation of due process. If you want to recall the reasons for that ruling, read more here.

Of course, critics hit what they described as a “grossly unfair” decision that sounded very didactic and which imposed new requirements for impeachment. It fueled perceptions of an interventionist Supreme Court that did not respect separation of powers.

More recently, Leonen, along with the majority, voted against a request for a temporary restraining order (TRO) sought by Senator Bato dela Rosa to block an arrest warrant issued against him by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity.

Caguioa also voted against the TRO, saying in his closing statement: “This case will define the Court. For too long, power has found ways to outrun justice. It has hidden in office, in influence, in violence, and now, in the language of due process. That ends here.”

The SC also recently voted unanimously against three petitions filed by supporters of the Vice President challenging the conviction threshold set by the impeachment court. Only 14 votes out of 20 active senator-judges will be required for a conviction of Sara Duterte, the impeachment court ruled.

Citing procedural grounds, the High Court junked the petitions, saying they were premature since no final judgment had been rendered and there was lack of legal standing. One of the petitions argued that senators who are still in office should be allowed to vote even if they are in hiding (Bato dela Rosa), detained (Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta), or have medical conditions (Loren Legarda).

Their inclusion would have set the voting base at 24 instead of 20 and raised the threshold to 16 for a Duterte conviction. The number 16 would be equivalent to two-thirds of “all the Members of the Senate” as required by the Constitution, the reasoning goes.

Nothing stops the petitioners from refiling their petitions but the unanimous decision already sends a strong signal that cannot be ignored. The impeachment trial court should have the final say on the voting threshold, seems to be the underlying message if you read the fine print.

Is the Supreme Court totally immune to political winds and oblivious to presidents? Perhaps not. But at a time when standards for choices of elective officials seem to be on the decline, many still look to the SC as a stronghold of justice and fairness to which high standards still apply. Has it lived up to those expectations? Let me know your thoughts.
After today’s interviews, the next set of chief justice candidates is scheduled on Monday, October 26, and will feature Associate Justices Rodil Zalameda, Japar Dimaampao, and Jose Midas Marquez.
Till Thursday after next!

articles.title: Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
articles.summary: New South Wales Police say inquiries took place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".

blocks.text: A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared.
"Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force."
BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received.
A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them."
Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments.

In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show.

One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us.
Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing".
As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4.
The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch.
In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.
The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.
The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 show.
The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.
The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.
Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published.
Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now".
BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response.
Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

articles.title: Is PH farmland healthy amid El Niño? FAO calls for soil assessment
articles.summary: With less frequent but more intense tropical cyclones expected in the coming months amid the El Niño phenomenon, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has called for soil assessment in the…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 5:45pm

With less frequent but more intense tropical cyclones expected in the coming months amid the El Niño phenomenon, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has called for soil assessment in the country's farmlands to ensure food security.
Dulce Carandang, FAO Philippines assistant representative for programme, said drought has other aspects other than low rainfall.
"Drought isn't just about the lack of rain. We also need to look at the state of our soil, the health of our groundwater," Carandang said during a press briefing in Makati City on Thursday.
"There may not be rain, but if our groundwater is really secure and it's available, then farmers would be able to produce food," she added.
Based on PAGASA's climate outlook for November 2026 to April 2027, there are 12 areas in the country predicted to experience drought in November.

The state weather bureau said drought occurs when there are three consecutive months of way below (>60% reduction from average) or five consecutive months of below normal (21%-60% reduction from average) rainfall condition.

blocks.caption: 'Drought isn't just about the lack of rain. We also need to look at the state of our soil, the health of our groundwater,' says Dulce Carandang, assistant representative for programme, Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) Philippines, during a press conference in Makati City on Thursday, Octo…

blocks.text: 'Drought isn't just about the lack of rain. We also need to look at the state of our soil, the health of our groundwater,' says Dulce Carandang, assistant representative for programme, Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) Philippines, during a press conference in Makati City on Thursday, October 22, 2026. MARIEL CELINE SERQUIÑA
Part of assessing the soil's health is its ability to absorb nutrients for plants, which could impact the food production.

"What we need to know with agricultural drought, which of course impacts on food production, 'yung, ano ba 'yun? Kamusta na 'yung soil health? Can it still absorb plants?" Carandang told GMA News Online in an interview.
According to the United States Department of Agriculture, soil health is the continued ability of soil to function as a living ecosystem that sustained plants, animals, and humans.
"It plays a critical role in regulating water, filtering pollutants, cycling nutrients, sustaining soil habitats, and promoting plant growth," the US agency said.
Carandang said the Bureau of Soils and Water Management is currently working with concerned agencies in gathering information about the country's state of vegetation.

"Climate science is evolving, it's progressing. And what is critical is that they (farmers) get all this updated information so that they know when to make the adjustment," the FAO official said during the press briefing.

The Department of Agriculture and the Philippine Space Agency recently signed a five-year agreement to use satellite technology to help monitor and protect farms and fishing areas from the effects of El Niño.
The satellite will monitor crop health, map flooding and dry spells, assess irrigation infrastructure, forecast harvests and identify areas at risk of agricultural damage. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: John Anderson, five-time US country chart-topper, dies aged 71
articles.summary:
Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila Night

John Anderson, the traditionalist US country singer whose extensive body of work…

blocks.text: John Anderson, the traditionalist US country singer whose extensive body of work included five No 1 hits on the country charts, has died aged 71.

The news was announced on social media by his family, who said: “To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely and made every ordinary moment feel special.”

So woven into the culture of country music that he once worked as a roofer on the genre’s focal point, Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry, Anderson’s career spanned nearly 50 years and resulted in him being inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024.

Among those paying tribute to Anderson was country singer and friend Blake Shelton: “I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be.” Shelton’s wife Gwen Stefani wrote: “We loved him!! His music is part of our family’s hearts for ever!!”

Born and raised in Florida in a music-loving family whose tastes spanned big band jazz to the Rolling Stones, Anderson headed to Nashville after graduating high school to try to make it in the city’s country music scene by playing live sets at night while doing manual labour during the day. “I’d fill up the truck with gravel and take the truck to wherever the order was and drop it off. A lot of odd jobs, but never lost sight of the fact that I really wanted to play,” he said in 2024.

Writing his own material as well as performing that of others, he released his debut single in 1975, but broke through two years later with I’ve Got a Feelin’ (Somebody’s Been Stealin’), and inched his way up the country charts with each subsequent release. He had his first country Top 5 single in 1981, I’m Just an Old Chunk of Coal (But I’m Gonna Be a Diamond Someday), which earned him his only Grammy nomination, for best male vocal country performance – and was a typical showcase of his wry, earnest and pure vocal tone.

It ushered in a number of years of commercial success, with the songs Wild and Blue, Black Sheep and Swingin’ all becoming country chart-toppers – the slick, hard-driving sound of the latter gave it crossover appeal and it became Anderson’s only hit on the US pop chart.

The latter half of the decade was a frustrating time for Anderson as he was dropped by his label Warner Bros and shuttled between others, before finding his groove again with 1992 album Seminole Wind, containing three Top 3 hits; the title track, an ode to his birth state of Florida, and Straight Tequila Night have endured as country radio staples and streaming successes. Follow-up Solid Ground was also a hit, containing the chart-topping Money in the Bank.

Anderson ended up recording 22 studio albums, most recently 2020’s Years, recorded with Dan Auerbach of blues-rockers the Black Keys. That was a proud and hard-fought return for Anderson, who faced illness with a non-cancerous tumour in 2017 that left him hospitalised. “I had been very, very ill,” he told Billboard in 2020. “I had almost 100% hearing loss … that really almost put an end to me. I just started praying and praying harder than I’ve ever prayed in my life and you know what? My hearing started coming back.”

Anderson continued to perform live thereafter, saying in 2024 that since his recovery, “I’ve really been enjoying every day. I live out in the woods and take a lot of lessons from my little wildlife friends. They pretty much live day to day, minute to minute. Enjoying that minute, enjoying this time. I’m very thankful to be able to go out and play any music at all.”

articles.title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
articles.summary: Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.

blocks.text: Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.
Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.

He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.

Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.

Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory.

There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.
More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.
So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.

On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.
In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.

Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.

For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.

articles.title: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
articles.summary: It is the latest in a series of attacks by the Houthi movement which have targeted airports and other sites in the kingdom.

blocks.text: Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says.
Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals.
The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles.
On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said.

The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze.
It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.
Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis' military spokesman said on Wednesday that they had targeted military equipment at an airport in the southern Yemeni city of al-Mukalla, which it said had been transported by Saudi Arabia for use by pro-government forces.
Meanwhile, Houthi-run media reported that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.
The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.
The UN says more than 256,000 people have also been displaced.

The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.
