articles.title: Entry ban a ‘small price to pay,’ says lawmaker on Chinese Embassy ‘list’
articles.summary: Ten lawmakers now want Marcos to expel the Chinese envoy or seek his recall.

blocks.text: October 22, 2026 | 4:08pm

MANILA, Philippines — Facing a travel ban to China is a “small price to pay” in exchange for standing up for Filipino fishers in the West Philippine Sea, a lawmaker said Tuesday, October 20, after the Chinese Embassy in Manila put him and others on a “list” of lawmakers implied as unwelcome in China.

Rep. Karl Legazpi (Pinoy Workers) issued the statement hours after the embassy reposted a joint statement by nine lawmakers urging the president to consider expelling Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan. The embassy had shared the lawmakers’ statement with the caption: “Put on record. You are now on the list.”

“If speaking up means foregoing the opportunity to visit a country I have always wanted to see, that is a small price to pay,” Legazpi said. “Some things are worth more than the privilege of being welcome.”

The embassy has not said what the list means and if it had any plans of formally barring the nine lawmakers from entering mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau, as was done with former Sen. Francis Tolentino, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., and more than a dozen Palawan municipal officials.

The sanction on Tolentino in July 2025 was the first time Beijing took state action against a specific critic in Manila, and in June this year China barred Teodoro, his spouse and his child from entering its territory and prohibited Chinese organisations and individuals from dealing with them.

Earlier in February, it banned 16 local government officials from the municipality of Kalayaan, Palawan, from entering mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macao. This was in retaliation for the persona-non-grata tag that the municipality — the country’s most remote and least populated town, located in the West Philippine Sea — had declared for China's ambassadors in 2023 and 2026.
An escalatory exchange of words between the embassy and officials followed after Jing, in a chance interview on October 15, told reporters: "If we want to use force, we may easily win."
The ambassador did not explicitly say that the use of force would be against Manila but the ambassador had delivered this response in reaction to Teodoro's remarks that China was a "troublemaker."
The Department of Foreign Affairs called Jing's remark a “thinly veiled threat," and Marcos said the next day that it “sounds very much to me like a threat."

The embassy did not retract the comment and accused the Philippine side of taking the ambassador's words out of context and overinterpreting them. It has since dared the Senate and the House to declare Jing persona non grata and “stop bluffing.”
On October 18, the embassy said those seeking his expulsion would not be welcome in China.
‘Somebody has to stand up’

“If I don’t speak up for my fellow Palaweños, who will?” Legazpi said in his statement Tuesday. “Rhetoric aside, benign or otherwise, the fact remains that our fishermen continue to be harassed and bullied by PRC vessels in waters where we have every legal right to fish, including our historical and traditional fishing grounds.”

“Kung may kapalit man ang paninindigang ito, so be it (If this stand comes at a cost, so be it),” Legazpi said, adding that he had “nothing against the Chinese people and their rich history and culture, which I have long admired.”
On Wednesday, October 21, ten House members filed House Resolution No. 1562 urging Marcos to either declare Jing persona non grata or ask Beijing to recall him.

Besides Legazpi, the authors are Reps. Ziaur-Rahman Alonto Adiong (Lanao del Sur), Adrian Michael Amatong (Zamboanga del Norte), Kaka Bag-ao (Dinagat Islands), Percival Cendaña (Akbayan), Chel Diokno (Akbayan) and Dadah Kiram Ismula (Akbayan), Leila de Lima (Mamamayang Liberal), Cielo Krisel Lagman (Albay) and Mark Anthony Santos (Las Piñas).
De Lima said that if the list referred to those who would not bend to Beijing’s narrative, she would be “honored and proud to be on the list."
Akbayan, whose three representatives were on the list, said it considered the designation an honor.

However, not all members of the House of Representatives have backed calls to expel Jing. The Makabayan bloc, through Reps. Antonio Tinio, Sarah Elago and Renee Co, urged all parties to de-escalate immediately and return to diplomacy, while continuing to assert the country’s sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea.
Rep. Edgar Erice (Caloocan City, 2nd District) urged Marcos to take personal charge of the dispute.
“Statements of bravado may sound good before television cameras and earn public applause, but foreign policy is not a shouting match,” Erice said.
He warned that a confrontation with China “without a clear strategic path could be disastrous for our already struggling economy."

articles.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use, as experts sound the alarm
articles.summary: The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far…

image.caption: In a bid to help farmers, the EU has proposed unlimited, open-ended approval for certain pesticidesImage: Andrii Yalanskyi/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.
Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of maximum 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities would bear the responsibility, not the industry.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and to help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.
Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?
The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances." But their stance still proposed extending initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.
The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation." He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.
How do pesticides affect human health, environment?
Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.
Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

blocks.caption: In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to the Agriculture MinistryImage: Adam Berry/Getty Images

blocks.text: When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides." However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: a survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time. "The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge."
More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe nongovernmental organization in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews. That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.
Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby. This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group, Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.
Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said. Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.
Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.
Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'?

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products. And that also includes maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides, not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but […] it will not be the silver bullet."

articles.title: Chancellor accepts Labour has put a ‘lot of pressure’ on business and that helping wealth creators will be budget aim – UK politics live
articles.summary:
John Healey is expected to cut red tape requirements, particularly for smaller businesses

Good morning. A week today John Healey, the chancellor, will be doing a media round…

blocks.text: Good morning. A week today John Healey, the chancellor, will be doing a media round defending the budget he is presenting on Wednesday next week. Ahead of that, he has given an interview to Patrick Maguire from the Times. As you would expect, there is no real detail in it about the measures he will be presenting to MPs. But the big picture message is very clear – and quite surprising, coming from a chancellor serving a PM who in some respects is steering left compared to his predecessor. Healey says that he wants to be on the side of bloody-minded entrepreneurs who make a profit, he acknowledges that government has made their life harder over the past two years, and he suggests that cutting the ‘cost of living’ for business is just as important as cutting the real cost of living for families.
In the quote that gives the Times its splash headline, Healey says:

double quotation markI want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, and those entrepreneurs who, in the end, are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures … If you’re not making a profit, you’ve got nothing to put back into the business. And for the people who start up these businesses, the ones who really thrive and grow, they have to make a profit — and they will be much more inclined to put it back into their own business. But we want it to grow here and stay here.

blocks.caption: Times splash. Photograph: The Times

blocks.text: And this is what he says about the government has recently been putting “a lot of pressure” on business.

double quotation markIf you talk to any of the businesses that have come in and have either had one-to-ones or round tables with me, I have recognised that in recent times there’s been a lot of pressure: employment law, regulation, tax, input costs, supply chains. And so when I talk about the cost of business, and recognising that in the same way as we’re recognising the cost of living pressures, I’m conscious of that as I go into the budget for both businesses and households.

All chancellors – including all Labour chancellors – say they want to help businesses make a profit. But many people in the business community suspect that, when they face fiscal pressure, Labour government will usually default to treating business as a cash machine.

Healey’s comments about wanting to be seen as “a chancellor who backs business” and about how tax rises and the Employment Rights Act have increased costs sound like an implicit rebuke to Rachel Reeves, his predecessor. In his interview Healey defends her decision to increase employer national insurance, saying she had to deal with the “dereliction of duty” of the last Tory government on the economy. But Healey still gives the impression of wanting to be seen as markedly more pro-business than Reeves.
In his interview Healey does not give details of how he will cut costs for business next week. But, in his write-up, Maguire says:

double quotation mark[Healey] is expected to use the budget to make significant cuts to regulation on businesses that one senior Treasury source described as “the sludge choking firms”. Reporting requirements are likely to be abolished for many smaller enterprises, The Times understands.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: The ONS publishes crime figures for England and Wales and – separately – annual gender pay gap figures.

10am: Ofgem chief executive Tim Jarvis and Department for Energy and Net Zero permanent secretary Jonathan Brearley give evidence to the Commons public accounts committee about achieving clean power by 2030.
10.15am: Kemi Badenoch gives a speech at the Police Federation’s annual conference.
Morning: Andy Burnham is in Manchester where he is getting a flu jab, and also holding a meeting with mayors at No 10 North about mayors retaining revenue from business rates.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
Lunchtime: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, speaks at a lunch at the Commons hosted by lobby journalists.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: West End to get another lesson from The History Boys two decades on
articles.summary:
Nation’s favourite play makes London comeback amid renewed debate about future of humanities teaching

The History Boys is to return to the West End for the first time in two decades, with a…
articles.byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent

blocks.text: The History Boys is to return to the West End for the first time in two decades, with a warning from its director of an “almost terminal decline” in humanities teaching in state schools.

Nicholas Hytner, who directed Alan Bennett’s play at the National Theatre and its 2006 film adaptation, said the themes of education, history and the value of literature for its own sake felt especially relevant amid renewed debate about what schools should teach.

“There has been a decline of humanities subjects in state schools, an almost terminal decline of music and drama teaching, history and modern languages have been downgraded,” he said. “But it has obviously been a mistake, both for the individual pupil and our economic future, to neglect the humanities.”
The production will open at the Theatre Royal Haymarket on 10 April for a 16-week run, reuniting Hytner with its original designer, Bob Crowley. Bennett will be involved in its development.

blocks.caption: Alan Bennett has welcomed the return of The History Boys, saying it was one of the happiest plays he had written. Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The Guardian

blocks.text: The History Boys received its world premiere at the National Theatre in 2004 before transferring to the West End and Broadway, where it won three Olivier awards and six Tonys. Voted the nation’s favourite play, it launched the careers of James Corden, Russell Tovey and Dominic Cooper.

Set in 1980s Sheffield, it follows eight boys at a grammar school preparing for their university entrance exams, as two teachers take opposing approaches to their education. Poignant and sharply comic, it explores adolescence, sexuality and the competing ideas of learning as a route to achievement or an end in itself.
Hytner said he had first asked Bennett whether he wanted to see the play revived: “He’s not usually that keen on revivals of his stuff, but he said he’d love to see it again.”

Bennett said: “The History Boys is one of the happiest plays I’ve written. Or rather, it was one of the happiest of my plays to write. It was also one of the quickest to set down, taking far less than my usual five years. So, something of a record for me. The play is full of quotes and has itself become eminently quotable. A joy for any playwright. I welcome its return under Nicholas Hytner.”

Its return comes as the government undertakes the first major revision of the national curriculum and GCSEs in more than a decade. Public consultations opened in September, with a revised curriculum expected in spring 2027 and implementation from 2028.

Hytner said: “It feels as if so much of what state education was focused on in the last 20 years is proving to be beside the point, when AI can do so much of what pupils were being prepared to do. Schools could do a lot worse than introduce pupils to creativity, and to delight in other people’s creativity.”

He said the play championed the idea that the humanities were “the birthright of anybody who goes through the school system”, rather than subjects whose value depended on their immediate practical application.

Hytner hopes it will resonate with a generation raised on social media. “Quite a lot of young people are ambivalent about social media,” he said. “They crave a kind of conversational spontaneity and an ability to concentrate and immerse themselves outside of social media.”
after newsletter promotion

The production will inevitably change, he added, having evolved between its opening at the National Theatre and the end of its Broadway run in 2006. Any changes, however, would be made with Bennett’s input.

blocks.caption: James Corden, Frances de la Tour and Richard Griffiths in the 2004 production. Photograph: Rex/Alastair Muir

blocks.text: Hytner emphasised the revival would again feature actors at the start of their careers: “I can almost guarantee that none of the new cast will be well-known figures, because that’s the point about them.”

He recalled that even the original cast had doubts about one of the play’s most farcical scenes, in which the teacher Hector gets his pupils to act out in French a client visiting a brothel in Paris. The charade ends with the headteacher entering the room while one of the boys has his trousers down.

“They were really suspicious of the French scene near the beginning of the play,” Hytner said. “Only a couple of them were confident about it, they just didn’t think it was funny. I had to keep saying it’s fine, let’s do it, let’s see how it goes.”
At the first preview, the scene brought the house down. “I remember the look of stunned amazement,” said Hytner. “It was a complete delight for the young actors.”

articles.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms
articles.summary: A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.
articles.byline: Dave Seglins, Andreas Wesley, Saloni Bhugra

image.caption: Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages, a new analysis shows. Most of them didn't include information about harm reduction or age restrictions. (David Zalubowski/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."
"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News.
His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but escalated.
One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.
T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.
"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."
Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.
Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211, a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.

items: Problem gambling jumps, suicides triple in Ontario after expansion of online casinos

blocks.text: 2-3 ads per minute
A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.
CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs to count the numbers of logos and gambling messages.
Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages. Ninety-five per cent of those instances included no information about harm reduction or age restrictions.

Raffaello Rossi, the lead researcher and a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol, says by reviewing every second of the game, his team found ads or logos appearing two to three times every minute.
Ads appeared on stadium rinks, jerseys, helmets and during commercial breaks.
Researcher found thousands of gambling messages in NHL games
"Advertising via logos around the stadium, on the jerseys, on the helmets is much more efficient, because you've got a lot of knock-on effects," he said.

"For example, if a news broadcast shows the highlights of a match, you will see these logos all across the sporting event. If somebody shares something on their social media, you will see those logos."
He says viewers are additionally seeing the emergence of ads for prediction markets.

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since a CBC Marketplace study with Rossi's team in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute).
Rossi says that's because Canada is behind other countries in passing legislation to curb gambling advertising.

"Multiple countries since then have introduced quite strict regulations and restrictions on gambling marketing in sports. So, for example, in Belgium and Italy and Spain, there's almost entire bans on sponsorship during sports."
Proposed Canadian ad standards
If Bill S-211 is approved at committee next week, the legislation — which has already passed the Senate — would be presented for a third and final reading in the House of Commons.
"It is a national framework around sports betting advertising," says the bill's sponsor, Bardish Chagger, the MP for Waterloo.

She says limits on advertising are a way to address emerging harms, including growing rates of gambling addiction and suicide deaths, like those witnessed in Ontario after the province allowed private online casinos and sports betting in 2022.

MP Bardish Chagger is sponsoring a bill launched by Sen. Marty Deacon to restrict gambling ads. The standing committee on Canadian heritage is set to vote on the bill in late October. (Dave Seglins/CBC)
"People are being impacted in a very harmful way. They are losing their livelihoods, they're losing their homes, they're losing their savings, they're losing their lives," Chagger told CBC News.
Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate and says it is time Canada tackles some of the negative public impacts of online gambling.

"These ads are ubiquitous across the country, especially in national broadcasts that are sponsored by betting companies, with logos plastered across broadcast desks, arenas and fields; this encourages Canadians in every province to gamble, even in those provinces who have held back," she wrote in an email to CBC News.
"We know where this is going, but we're allowing it to happen anyway."
Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate, where it has passed. (Twitter)
Current Canadian regulations are supposed to restrict gambling advertising targeting minors, at-risk people and gamblers who have asked to be excluded from the sites.
But the code doesn't go as far as some European countries, which have outright banned televised promotions on sportswear and during events.
Belgium, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany have imposed time-of-day bans on gambling advertisements, restricting them to after 9 p.m.
In France, companies have to get approval for their promotional strategies from the regulatory authority and submit an annual action plan to curb addiction.
While Canada's Bill S-211 isn’t prescriptive, it asks the federal government to acknowledge the harms of online gambling and hold consultations to craft stricter regulations.
Toronto Maple Leafs celebrate a goal flanked by advertising for Jackpot City online casino. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Chagger says she hopes her bill will eventually lead to a ban on gambling promotions on sportswear and during live sporting events, outlaw ads during certain hours and prohibit celebrities and athletes from collaborating with gambling companies.
Ontario and Alberta oppose the federal bill.
In a letter to the federal government, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Dale Nally said the bill creates a two-tier regulatory system and threatens future profits.
Ontario's Attorney General Doug Downey wrote to the federal government earlier this year, saying that the province should be left to regulate ads.

"Ontario has already established comprehensive and modern regulatory framework for online gaming and sports betting, which came into force in 2022. Advertising standards and protections were a central component of this work," he wrote.
Public health response

A coalition of a dozen mental health organizations, including the Canadian Mental Health Association and Public Health Physicians of Canada, alongside 28 prominent addictions researchers, have sent submissions to Parliament asking for national action.
"The entire world is grappling with this in some way," said Matthew Young, a leading gambling researcher and senior research associate at the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction.
"The real challenge right now is that we have a regulatory regime that is built upon physical borders, but a product that doesn't respect physical borders."
Addictions researcher Matthew Young is lobbying for limits on gambling ads and better monitoring of harms. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)
"The argument that it's provincial and territorial jurisdiction was all fine and well until ads from Ontario blanketed the nation and then suddenly New Brunswick had to deal with ads from Ontario."

The Canadian Gaming Association (CGA), a national trade group representing 80 companies that run casinos and online sports betting, has filed its own submission opposing the plan to regulate gambling ads across the country.
Instead, the CGA wants the government to spend money on assessing the "underlying health challenges" of gambling addiction, and let provinces decide advertising standards for themselves."

items: CBC Marketplace 2024 study of gambling ads

blocks.text: "Unlike alcohol and cannabis, online gambling platforms, both regulated and unregulated, are readily accessible with just a few clicks. In this environment, advertising plays an important role in directing consumers toward regulated operators that are subject to stringent oversight, consumer protection requirements and responsible gambling standards," the CGA submission states.
Recovering gambler T.S. says advertising for online casino games should be banned or require warnings, similar to rules for other addictive substances, like tobacco and alcohol.
"I think similar to cigarettes, you could put labelling on the apps themselves, as well as the ads: 'Here's what happened to Terry when he spent half his life savings on blackjack one night.'"

articles.title: Politics is widening U.S. gender divides. In Canada? It's complicated
articles.summary: Young men and women tell CBC's The House that politics plays a big role in who they choose to date — as the political divide along gender lines become a major issue south of the border.

image.caption: Young men and women tell CBC's The House that politics plays a big role in who they choose to date — as the political divide along gender lines become a major issue south of the border. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Young men and women tell CBC's The House that politics plays a big role in who they choose to date — as the political divide along gender lines become a major issue south of the border.
Polling shows Canada's youth aren't feeling the same divides as their southern neighbours
Connor Halloran says his last relationship wasn't entirely quashed by a disagreement with his now ex-partner over politics, but it was "almost the last straw."
Halloran said his past partner's contradictory views "made me judge her a little differently in a way that I didn't really want to be around her as much anymore."
He's not alone — at least on the University of Ottawa campus, where most students either said politics is pivotal in their relationships or that they avoid bringing it up altogether.
CBC Radio's The House caught Halloran and his friend and fellow geography major Alex Kelly as they stepped out onto a campus sidewalk after an exam on Wednesday.
Kelly maintains it's best to keep politics out of dating to "avoid conflict and confrontation."
"Is that kind of living in secrecy? Maybe a little bit," Kelly said. "But, I mean, [if] you want a long-lasting relationship, I think sometimes a little bit of secrecy is good — maybe."
Alex Kelly, left, and Connor Halloran, right, spoke to CBC Radio's The House on Oct. 14 at the University of Ottawa. (David Cummings/CBC)

The cautious sentiments are "very familiar" to Daniel Cox, the director of the Survey Center on American Life, who, in his most recent book, looks at how politics has impacted some youths' dating lives as a symptom of a larger social trend.
"There is this incredible wariness about dating someone even with a little bit of a different political take or whose identity didn't quite align," Cox told The House.
In Generation Uncoupled, Cox examines the growing political divide among young American women and men. Cox says he interviewed over 100 people whose personal stories his book relies on.
"It's not necessarily that young men are becoming more conservative, but young women are becoming much, much more liberal," he said.
In his research, Cox said he found social media plays a role in fragmenting young Americans along gender lines.

items: Kids and young adults are addicted to screens. New research argues it may be a public health concern

blocks.text: "When it comes to the algorithms, they are both very, very powerful and they are better able to identify gender than almost any other attribute," Cox said.

"So young men and young women have very different experiences when they're on the same social media platforms, and their realities are shaped by this understanding, this sort of validation machine that is affirming their perspectives, experiences and point of view."

Cox also points to the divisive politics of U.S. President Donald Trump, in a chapter titled The Divider in Chief, and told The House the president serves as the biggest dealbreaker "by a landslide" when it comes to young people's relationships.

"When I talked to a lot of young women who said that they could not date a Trump supporter, his policies never really came up," Cox said. "Rather it was his demeaning comments about women, belittling behaviour, his history of sexual assault allegations."

items: U.S. Supreme Court again rejects Trump's effort to overturn E. Jean Carroll verdict

blocks.text: According to Andrew Parkin, executive director of the Environics Institute For Survey Research, youth aren't feeling the same split north of the border.
"People in the U.S. are reacting to their political developments," Parkin told The House. "We haven't had a leader like Trump to provoke that kind of reaction to see what would happen."

Parkin pointed to a longstanding polling trend of young women tending to lean a bit more toward the left than young men, who generally lean a little more socially conservative, saying the difference has "been there for a while, and it's not growing."

items: How young men are changing what conservatism looks like in Canada

blocks.text: "Men are not generally becoming more conservative," he said.

"To the extent that there's a gender difference among younger people, between young men and young women, it'll be women that are a little bit more dissatisfied" with government and the political system.
Can love really be blind — to politics?
The House also checked in with Melissa and Conrad Muhly, a couple living just outside of Philadelphia.

Since the start of their 25 years of marriage, a once trivial political wrinkle between them has grown in significance: Melissa is a dual Canada-U.S. citizen and has been voting Democrat while Conrad voted for Trump.
LISTEN | Melissa and Conrad's previous appearance on The House:
The House48:48Elbows up, Canada
Conrad said politics "matters significantly" when it comes to relationships.

Melissa said political differences weren't a big deal when they started dating 26 years ago, adding, "these days it feels almost like your political views become part of your value system and your soul."

"Now, we have a great marriage, a great relationship for both of us," Conrad said. "For someone starting out, I think to have [such] diametric views, it would be very difficult to have a relationship."
"I think that it would be very tough for a couple newly dating to navigate these waters," Melissa said. "We've been able to do it, but it hasn't always been easy."
Asked whether they would end up married had they met today, Melissa didn't mince words: "absolutely not.… In fact, I wouldn't date a Republican, if I'd known what one was 25 years ago."
"I would, you know, try to sway my significant other at the time to see the right side of things, and if she did, we would get along fine," Conrad responded, as they both chuckled.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada
articles.summary: The Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, from Canadian comedian and director Nathan Fielder, is taking the world by storm. A grocery list of Canadian creatives are behind it.

image.caption: Nathan Fielder speaks onstage at the You Can See Everything premiere during the 64th New York Film Festival at Alice Tully Hall, Lincoln Center on Sept. 30, 2026 in New York City. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, from Canadian comedian and director Nathan Fielder, is taking the world by storm. A grocery list of Canadian creatives are behind it.
The Elizabeth Holmes doc is vying for top spot at the Oscars. A number of Canadian names got it there
If you're aware of Nathan Fielder, you're probably aware he, in his resoundingly patriotic words, "graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades."

Which — despite the intentionally ridiculous way it's read out in the intro to his show Nathan for You — is true: The Canadian comedian really did get his bachelor of commerce at the University of Victoria, before eventually transitioning to that show, known for its farcically absurd business advice.

It might seem random to connect Canadian business school with obsessive investigations and near-incomparable success. But that background established a pattern for the Vancouver-born Fielder. Since the earliest days of his comedy career, Fielder has built what basically amounts to an entire field of study around the fickle nature of truth.

Practically all his work has been undergirded by this concept, from his early days at CBC's This Hour Has 22 Minutes to the more mind-bendingly bizarre The Curse and The Rehearsal and all the way to the world's hottest documentary right now: the Elizabeth Holmes-focused You Can See Everything, which released last Friday.

But as odd as those releases seem, they have created something of a cottage industry around Fielder, and the belief he is turning the format of documentary on its head. The film's run-and-gun-style employed an incredibly small team of roughly seven on-site crew members, a significant number of which, like Fielder, hail from Canada. And given the tradition of documentary in this country — as well as the fact that this time, he's not doing it alone — the movie's success may not seem so odd after all.
Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes appears in a still from Nathan Fielder's mindbending documentary You Can See Everything. (A24)
Unreal success

The most prominent Canadian of You Can See Everything is, of course, Fielder himself. He first rose to fame with his show, Nathan for You, a Comedy Central expansion of a segment that he established on 22 Minutes.
That series was what led the documentary's co-director, Lance Oppenheim, to approach Fielder about working on a project together in the first place, according to an interview with Vulture.

From there, Oppenheim and Fielder brought in their respective collaborators. On Fielder's end, that included Adam Locke-Norton, the editor with whom he first collaborated for shorts like Morris, Flashback and Eves, released on YouTube in 2006.

Meanwhile, Oppenheim brought in his own team, supported by the Great White North. That included Ottawa-born producer Tatiana Bears, who told CBC News she flew to the location just 24 hours after getting Oppenheim's call to start shooting. There was also director of photography David Bolen, a Toronto native who was the cinematographer for Oppenheim's narrative debut Primetime and his prior, self-styled "documentary fantasy" creations Spermworld and Some Kind of Heaven.
Bolen's camera was a particularly mind-bending aspect of You Can See Everything, fuelling much of its Oscars buzz.

items: Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes
Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'

blocks.text: Further down the line, there are more names: Saskatchewan's Katina Danabassis was in charge of costuming. Described by Vogue Philippines as "one of A24’s most radical collaborators," her oeuvre stretches from fellow Canadian Celine Song's Materialists and Past Lives to Fielder's The Curse, as well as this year's The Drama.

And then Ontario filmmaker Stephen Coleman — who previously worked on A24 projects Materialists, The Drama and the upcoming Jesse Eisenberg film The Debut — lent his hand as second assistant director.

They are now among those listed in A24's "for your consideration" Oscars campaign: Danabassis for best costume design, Bolen for best cinematography, Bears for the coveted best picture and Locke-Norton for best editing. Fielder and Oppenheim are submitted for best director.

A24 is also submitting You Can See Everything in the documentary category, but it may be angling for a record with best picture: If successful, it would become the first documentary to garner a nomination in that category.
Canadians in Hollywood

Canadians finding their way into Hollywood productions is by no means a new phenomenon. The United States has offered a fertile and appetizing landing pad to well-trained anglophone Canadian creatives without a thriving homegrown industry of their own. But A24, which funded You Can See Everything, has been establishing itself as both a home for, and source of, Canadian talent.

The distribution studio behind films like Backrooms, Everything Everywhere All at Once and Moonlight is infamously experimental, having enough faith in Fielder's vision that it signed a contract allowing him to cancel the project at any time, consequence-free.

Early this year, the studio released Undertone, the ultra low-budget, Toronto-shot horror from Montreal director Ian Tuason that earned more than $20 million US worldwide. It also nabbed the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, directed by Canada's Matt Johnson. That film had a surprisingly strong $5-million US wide debut, following a prior limited release, and eventually grossed nearly $20 million US worldwide.

That incursion hasn't been without friction. Along with a perceived shift away from risk-taking indie fare, A24 was recently in hot water over pulling the Canadian-directed Tony from an independent Toronto theatre over a "clearance issue." That practice, orchestrated and overseen by distributors but kept alive by large cinema chains' superior market share, keeps smaller theatres from being able to play the same film as nearby larger ones.

items: Ian Tuason haunted his own house when making his new horror film

blocks.text: Still, a supposed turn to Canadian talent could make awards sense. And when it comes to success at the Academy, there is one place Canada has historically shown considerable strength: the world of documentary filmmaking.

The term "documentary" itself was coined by critic John Grierson in 1926, who would go on to create Canada's National Film Board. Meanwhile, the Quebec-set 1922 film Nanook of the North is widely cited as the first feature-length documentary. Though many scenes in the latter were staged, the early connections have bloomed into recurrent Oscars success.

A Canadian documentary feature — producer Guy Glover's The Stratford Adventure — was first nominated at the 1955 ceremony. The country's first documentary feature win came in 1976 with The Man Who Skied Down Everest, followed by CBC's Just Another Missing Kid in 1983 and most recently for a wholly Canadian production with Artie Shaw: Time Is All You've Got. It tied for a win in 1987.

Nominations are more frequent: as recently as Julian Brave NoiseCat's Sugarcane (co-directed with Emily Kassie) for the 2025 ceremony and Nisha Pahuja's To Kill a Tiger at the 2024 awards. Numerous other Canadian-crafted films have also made their way to the Academy Awards, such as Daniel Roher's 2022 film Navalny, or the 2002 Michael Donovan co-produced Bowling for Columbine.

In the best documentary short category, Canadians are even more representative: Since 2011, at least 10 films by Canadians have been nominated. Of those, four have won. Conversely, no wholly Canadian movie has ever been nominated for or won best picture — though Canadian filmmakers James Cameron and Paul Haggis have won for Titanic and Crash, respectively.
In the international category, in which Canada is more routinely competitive, only Denys Arcand has won: for The Barbarian Invasions in 2004 (the category was then called best foreign language film).
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Biologists seek justice for forgotten kingdom of fungi
articles.summary: This week a UN summit aims to preserve the world's plants and animals. But a group of scientists wants to protect another diverse kingdom of species they say are too often forgotten – fungi. Here's a…

image.caption: Chilean mycologist Giuliana Furci, executive director of the Fungi Foundation, examines fungi in Tierra del Fuego. (Mateo Barrenengoa)

blocks.text: As world leaders meet at a UN summit to preserve the world's animals and plants, a group of scientists is pushing to protect another diverse kingdom of species they say is too often forgotten – fungi.

The fungi on Earth weigh six times more than the world's animals combined, and there are an estimated 5 million species, ranging from edible mushrooms to microscopic organisms that play essential roles in ecosystems.
"Without fungi, the world as we know [it] wouldn't exist," says Chilean mycologist Giuliana Furci.
Yet fungi traditionally haven't been included in efforts to protect plants and animals — something that struck her years ago.

"When I realized they weren't incorporated into environmental legislation, the sense of injustice was so profound," recalled Furci. Her response was to create the Fungi Foundation, which she believes is the first non-profit organization dedicated to conserving the world's fungi, in 2012.

Since then, others have popped up — including Canada-based Mycosphaera — together forming the Global Fungal Conservation Network. On Wednesday, the coalition launched the Global Strategy for Fungal Conservation at the COP17 UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia.
Jack-o'-lantern mushroom in Wolfville, N.S. (Submitted by Allison Walker)

The UN meeting is checking progress on the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, a global agreement to protect 30 per cent of the world's land, inland waters and marine areas by 2030 and mobilize billions of dollars in annual funding for biodiversity.

items: Canada led a 2022 deal to protect the world's nature. Has there been progress since then?

blocks.text: While the agreement explicitly mentions the need to balance the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems, fungi are not mentioned.
Tetrapyrgos alba. (Carolina Magnasco/Fungi Foundation)
Furci said talking about flora and fauna without fungi is "obsolete," since they were recognized as a separate kingdom in 1969 — and they're key to the survival of many plants and animals.

"Fungi are organisms that play such a significant role in the environment ... that leaving them out gives us a completely incomplete picture of life on Earth and ecosystem functions, and how we can tackle the diverse crises that we're facing, from climate change to biodiversity loss," she said ahead of her travel to COP17.
Cortinarius magellanicus, found in South America and New Zealand. (Giuliana Furci/Fungi Foundation)
Many are nameless, uncounted
Allison Walker first noticed wild mushrooms of all shapes, sizes and colours as a small child camping with her family in Algonquin Park.
"I would come up with names for them, like 'Donut Brothers' or 'Pancake King,'" she recalled.
Many fungi don't, in fact, have "real names," said Walker, now a biology professor at Acadia University in Wolfville, N.S., since fewer than five per cent have been formally described.
Unidentified fungi growing on a branch. (Catalina Infante/Fungi Foundation)

But the fungi scientists are tracking face threats just as plants and animals do. Last March, the IUCN Red List, which assesses and tracks extinction risk for species worldwide, had added 1,300 fungi, at least 411 of which were threatened with extinction.
The number of fungi assessed is still just a tiny fraction of the 96,000 animals and 176,000 plants on the list.
Furci said fungi face many of the same threats as other organisms, including fungicides, fertilizers, habitat fragmentation, habitat loss and climate change.
"Nevertheless," she said, "we have never looked to tailor actions … to ensure their survival."
Furci says doing so wouldn't just benefit fungi themselves.

"Plants can't live outside of water without fungi on their roots," she said. "Herbivores can't digest the plant they eat without the fungi in their stomachs.… We depend on fungi hugely for food, medicine, and many other things."
Witch's cauldron in northern B.C. (Cynthia Andal)
Fungi also play essential roles in decay and recycling nutrients.
Walker said that because so many other organisms rely on fungi, understanding those relationships is often important for habitat restoration – and can help explain why some restoration projects fail.

In Canada, Walker said fungal species that may be at risk include witch's cauldron in northern B.C., which resembles a giant black puffball, and the pepper pot earthstar, a species that's been only found four times in southwestern Ontario.
Pepper pot earthstar (Myriostoma coliforme), found only four times in southwestern Ontario. (Submitted by Allison Walker)
"It looks like a little star, but also like a pepper shaker because it has these little holes in the middle to release spores … kind of charismatic and cute."
Hard to identify and count
Walker acknowledged there are challenges to protecting rare fungi. Not only do we not know what fungal species are out there, but they can also be very hard to count.
"It's hard to say … what is actually rare versus just understudied."
Many species are microscopic, including those Walker studies in the roots of Spartina grasses that grow in salt marshes.
"Sometimes, you know, it requires a lot of hours at the microscope to tell apart different species."
Allison Walker looks at microscopic fungi found in the roots of salt marsh grasses. (Submitted by Allison Walker)
The fungi contain proteins that aren't found in the grass itself and that stain blue. (Allison Walker)

Many live underground, and even those that produce visible mushrooms above ground don't necessarily fruit every year. Some may produce mushrooms only under specific conditions, such as after a wildfire.

The underground network of cells making up one genetic individual can also stretch many kilometres and produce mushrooms over a wide area, making it difficult to measure the actual abundance of a species.
"It's very different from counting animals and plants."
Initiatives at COP
Still, conservationists are trying.

At the UN biodiversity conference two years ago, the Fungi Foundation proposed a fungal conservation pledge that has been signed by 15 countries. More are expected to sign on during the second week of COP17.
Canada hasn't yet signed, but Walker and other Canadian mycologists have been pushing for it to join.
Mycena epipterygia. (Giuliana Furci/Fungi Foundation)
The countries that signed the pledge have already helped get fungi included in scientific recommendations to signatories of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity.

Furci said greater recognition of fungi within the UN agreement could help countries incorporate them into biodiversity monitoring, conservation planning, ecosystem restoration and national biodiversity strategies.
Ramaria flava. (Giuliana Furci/Fungi Foundation)
But Furci thinks average people can also make a difference by learning about fungi and acknowledging their importance in everyday life.
"Language creates reality," she said. "To start talking about fungi alongside plants and animals is the first solid step that everybody can do and should do."

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

articles.title: Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing could lose prison privileges under new rules
articles.summary:
England and Wales judges will be able to keep inmates in their cells for longer or stop visits if they refuse to face their victims’ families in court

Offenders who refuse to face their…

blocks.text: Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales.

The imposition of new prison sanctions, coming into effect next year, build on existing laws that order offenders to attend sentencing or face a fine or be jailed for a further two years for contempt of court.

“Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences,” said prisons minister Catherine McKinnell.

The new rules, to be laid before parliament on Thursday, will grant judges new powers to impose a loss of prison privileges for 84 days, cell confinement for 21 days, a loss of social visits for 27 days and a restriction on visits to once every four weeks, for 84 days. They could result in offenders already facing decades behind bars facing additional punishments.

The Ministry of Justice has said that while no measure can guarantee offenders will attend their sentencing hearing, the widened powers strengthen the consequences for offenders and ensure they can be “appropriately punished”.

Younger offenders aged 18 to 20 could have privileges removed for up to 21 days or be confined to cells for up to 10 days, said the MoJ. Visitors from prisoners’ children will be exempt, to help maintain family ties and when in the child’s best interests.

Claire Waxman, the victim’s commissioner for England and Wales, who has worked with the families of Sabina Nessa, Zara Aleena and Jan Mustafa, said the announcement reflected the “tireless efforts” of victims’ families.
“I know how offenders’ refusal to attend sentencing hearings compounds trauma and robs families of one of the very few moments of accountability in the justice process,” said Waxman.
“It is now essential that these powers are used consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve,” she added.
after newsletter promotion
The move comes after nearly 2,000 prisoners across England and Wales were released from prison this month, in a government plan to ease prison overcrowding.

French president Emmanuel Macron is back from his tour of the Gulf and convening a meeting with relevant…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Macron hosts a security council meeting on protests

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

French president Emmanuel Macron is back from his tour of the Gulf and convening a meeting with relevant ministers and intelligence services to figure out what can be done to prevent unsavoury scenes on the streets of French cities as more protests are planned for this Saturday.

blocks.caption: French president Emmanuel Macron gestures as he speaks to members of the media on his Gulf trip. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters

blocks.text: “The government must hold its nerve,” Macron told reporters earlier this week.
He is expected to speak after the meeting, so once to watch.
Later today, French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a separate meeting with party leaders to discuss their concerns, including about policing and the next year’s presidential campaign.

blocks.caption: French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu seen here during a session of Questions to the Government in Paris, France. Photograph: Szwarc Henri/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Over in Ukraine, there are no signs of Russian attacks stopping anytime soon, after a night of “massive strikes” on port infrastructure facilities in Odesa region and on Kyiv.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andii Sybiha commented on the attacks, saying:

“Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential areas. Other cities across Ukraine came under attack as well. Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
No prizes for guessing who he may be addressing these comments to.
I will also bring you the latest from Serbia where the last day of campaigning begins before this Sunday’s closely contested parliamentary election.
Lots for us to cover.
It’s Thursday, 22 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: nowThailand, Malaysia urge citizens to avoid protest-hit EU countries
7m agoMorning opening: Macron hosts a security council meeting on protests

blocks.text: Thailand, Malaysia urge citizens to avoid protest-hit EU countries
Thailand has advised its citizens to postpone non-essential travel to parts of Europe rocked by protests, while Malaysia also warned its nationals about visiting France, AFP reported.

blocks.caption: People walk past a shop with its display windows protected by wooden panels in Paris, France. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters

blocks.text: “Those travelling from Thailand to Europe must closely monitor the situation as it is changing rapidly and France remains a concern as the situation is still ongoing,” Thai foreign minister Sihasak Phungketkeow told reporters late Wednesday during a trip to Italy.

He cited concerns about protests in Italy, noting his Italian counterpart had to cancel their bilateral due to an urgent government cabinet meeting on the unrest, adding: “We are also worried about Spain.”
“If it’s not necessary, with everything going on in those countries, I think it’s better to delay the trip for a while.”
The Malaysian embassy in Paris had on Sunday advised Malaysians in France “to exercise caution and remain vigilant” due to the protests.
China warned its citizens travelling to France to take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported Monday, after town halls and shops were looted and set on fire at the weekend.

articles.title: Asian governments step up cyber defenses after PHP flaw
articles.summary: The rush comes after government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline, with the disclosure of the PHP flaws sending website operators scrambling to protect their systems

blocks.text: Companies and governments around the world raced on Thursday, October 22, to patch vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP programming language, as experts reported a surge in hacking attempts following their disclosure.
The rush came after government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday, with the disclosure of the flaws sending website operators scrambling to protect their systems.

PHP developers on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying all users were “encouraged to update immediately.”

“In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Matthew Prince, the CEO of cloud services firm Cloudflare, said in a post on social media platform X late on Wednesday.
“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”

Japanese lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group said on Thursday it was temporarily suspending some internet services due to emergency measures. Japan’s Finance Ministry also suspended some website content and online services while implementing security measures.
Several governments across Asia ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP flaw on Thursday.

China’s industry ministry urged organizations and users to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP. It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and promptly changing accounts, passwords and keys.

South Korea’s government raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures over the flaw, citing concerns about an increased risk of hacking attacks. – Rappler.com

articles.title: View from Manila: Making sense of the gutter talk from China’s embassy
articles.summary: ‘Let the good aspects prevail over bad ones. Otherwise we may easily fall into the situation of countermeasures and retaliation,’ China’s envoy says. Yet his taunts seem to be sending a different…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Before the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over a remark that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself perceived as a “threat,” the Chinese embassy made perfectly clear how it viewed the avalanche of criticism toward it from all corners of the Philippine government: with unmistakable bravado.

In an October 18 post, a day before Jing was summoned by Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma Theresa Lazaro, the embassy said: “Some anti-China politicians talked about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata (PNG). Over the past 30 years, anti-China forces have been repeatedly doing the same thing to threaten our embassy.”

“We are fed up with these old and low tricks. If they really want to do something, do it quickly and immediately, please. While diplomacy is based on reciprocity, we will not welcome them to China. Simple and fair enough.”

The embassy’s public dare for legislators to pass persona non-grata resolutions has resulted in precisely that — the filing of resolutions calling on either Marcos to expel Jing or the DFA to recommend his expulsion, or for the executive to ask China to recall Jing Quan.

These resolutions are symbolic. Congress cannot actually compel Marcos or the DFA to kick Jing out of the Philippines, although they can raise the public stakes further by calling for legislative hearings on the matter.
But the resolutions tighten what little wiggle room Marcos has — domestically, bilaterally, or diplomatically — to find an elegant offramp for both Manila and Beijing for the current diplomatic row.
That is, unless an expulsion of Jing — or at least calls for it — is what Beijing wants at such a delicate time for Manila.

Taunting Philippine politicians publicly and causing a maelstrom on both social media and diplomatic spaces now obfuscate a core issue: that both countries have supposedly agreed on rules to follow in maritime spaces, based on international law. China has repeatedly disregarded these rules when it’s convenient. It muddles an already murky discourse — making it even harder to keep track of, and losing nuance.
It also tests how the rest of the world — Manila’s friends and allies included — would react to what would be a downgrade in bilateral ties between China and the Philippines.

In a release on Lazaro’s summoning of Jing, the DFA said: “It is not the place of a foreign mission to publicly criticize or taunt Philippine officials and legislators who are acting within their mandates. As a democracy, the Philippines values freedom of expression and a plurality of voices, and it will not accept attempts by a foreign envoy to intimidate those who exercise them.”
Yet, deeper and deeper into the gutter the Chinese embassy has gone.
As of posting, the embassy has posted variations of the following:

items: Declaring House lawmakers who called for the expulsion of Jing as being “on the list.” Pressed by the media to expound on what that meant, an embassy official said, “At least they are not welcome to China.” Does that mean they’re sanctioned the same way as Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.? For this, China’s diplomats had no response.
Mocking several senators — including Senator JV Ejercito who had apparently once endorsed a China-made vehicle — for their comments against China.

The embassy has also sneered at the DFA itself, and Senator Francis Pangilinan. “Using thuggish, hooligan-style language to launch personal attacks on others — is this the calibre and standards of a Philippine senator? Is this the diplomacy and prudence that the DFA claims to uphold?” the embassy said in a post.

In responding to Senator Panfilo Lacson’s call for the DFA to “politely [ask China] to recall [Jing],” the embassy replied: “MESSAGE TO DFA: Holding Philippine high-ranking elected officials accountable for reckless, inflammatory remarks and constantly smearing and maligning a neighboring country and urging them to watch their words and handle matters diplomatically is about preserving bilateral relations. It is not a failure of diplomacy.”

blocks.text: In a statement on Thursday, October 22, the DFA said the embassy’s “escalatory and undiplomatic tone and language used in the latest social media statements…erode mutual trust and confidence, and severely undermine the efforts to stabilize and improve bilateral relations.”
“All diplomats are expected to conduct and express themselves in a manner befitting diplomatic envoys, especially on social media,” said the DFA.

blocks.caption: View from Manila: Mr. President, put order in your West Philippine Sea house

blocks.text: China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said little on the back-and-forth in Manila.

“To improve and develop China-Philippines relations serves the interest of both sides. We firmly oppose certain Philippine individuals maliciously lashing out at China and hurting bilateral ties. The Philippine side should rein in such irresponsible behavior of those politicians,” its spokesperson Mao Ning said on October 19.

It’s assumed that the embassy and its diplomats understand that under the Philippine system, legislators belong to a separate branch of government. Neither senators nor lawmakers report to the DFA — at best, they consult. It’s Congress that deliberates and has oversight on the DFA’s budget, the same way it does the budget of other executive agencies, including Malacañang (and the Office of the Vice President).

It would be far-fetched to consider that the Chinese embassy’s provocations are done without the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or the Chinese government’s permission or encouragement — whether it be passive or pro-active. It would be unthinkable for any embassy to have gone rogue from the wishes of its home office and government for this long a time — the harsh, sometimes uncouth statements from the embassy have been a hallmark of Jing’s tenure, beginning in late 2025.

Before being assigned to Manila, Jing was deputy chief of mission of China’s embassy in Washington DC. Before that, he was a minister in the same post. He’s been described as an expert on US-China ties, above all. Jing was reportedly on call for Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump’s summits in Beijing and Washington DC.

His assignment to Manila is by design. Bilateral ties between the Philippines and the United States have flourished under Marcos, especially when it comes to defense and security. Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) sites have nearly doubled under his administration, and US foreign military financing allocations for the Philippines stands at $2.5 billion across five years until 2031, after a $500 million pledge in 2024.

American weapons — the Typhon and the NMESIS — were brought in for use in the annual Balikatan wargames and have yet to leave Philippine shores. Trade and industrial ties — through the Luzon Economic Corridor and Pax Silica — are hoped to only grow between the two countries.

Growing closer to the US has also meant expanding Manila’s strategic and security ties — countries that are also close partners of Washington, such as Japan. These moves have been unsettling for Beijing.

In their media release on Lazaro’s summon, Jing defended his original remarks by saying he was only pushing for a “differentiated approach to handle the problems of various sectors, based on their own merits instead of linking one to another.”

The Chinese ambassador added: “We should enhance dialogue, manage differences and deepen cooperation, create more good stories, good news. Let the good aspects prevail over bad ones. Otherwise we may easily fall into the situation of countermeasures and retaliation.”
But kicking Jing out is the nuclear option, at least diplomatically.

What follows could be reciprocal or disproportionate — from kicking out Manila’s ambassador to Beijing to imposing trade sanctions that they’ve already threatened to do in the past. Either outcome can only escalate tensions in the region.

Manila and Beijing’s relationship has been tense for decades — especially post-2012 or after a standoff in Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal) that ended with China having the upperhand. The relationship soured even more in 2013, after Manila took Beijing to court — and walked away victorious years later, with the 2016 Arbitral Award.

Then-president Rodrigo Duterte, who wanted closer ties with Beijing, set that award aside. Under Duterte, Manila was Beijing’s darling — even as it meant that little was said of the landmark award publicly and maritime units were extra cautious in the West Philippine Sea.

Marcos did a 180 by making the 2016 Arbitral Award front and center in its maritime, defense, and foreign policy. On the defense side, ties are closest with nations that recognize and actively support the landmark ruling.

A transparency initiative from 2023 to 2024 put Chinese harassment on the international stage — footage of the China Coast Guard (CCG) harassing its Philippine counterparts made the rounds regularly on the news and online. This helped rally support for the Philippines from allies and friends old and new — but did little to actually stop and manage Chinese harassment.

The situation simmered in mid-2024, after a tense confrontation at the foot of the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin (Second Thomas Shoal), which resulted in the loss of one Filipino soldier’s thumb and damage to military equipment.

Between 2024 and early-2026, incidents sprang up here and there — to include aerial confrontations and numerous maritime confrontations. But things boiled over again in 2026, or just as Jing got his feet wet as the new envoy to Manila.
As his embassy’s rhetoric grew bolder, so did incidents in the West Philippine Sea.

The CCG approached the BRP Sierra Madre in July 2026, supposedly to check if construction had taken place. Jing claimed that under a provisional arrangement, the details of which are confidential, the Philippines is not allowed to bring construction materials. Lazaro, who was undersecretary for bilateral affairs when the temporary arrangement was made in 2024, said this was not the case.

In late September 2025, a resupply mission to Ayungin was reportedly hindered by the CCG. Weeks later, a medical evacuation for a soldier with a ruptured appendix was stalled for hours because the CCG refused to let the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) get closer to the BRP Sierra Madre.

The July incident happened just as Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi made a quick trip to Manila for the ASEAN Foreign Ministers meetings. Beijing accused the Philippines of, somehow, orchestrating a confrontation that led to the injury of one soldier.

The September and October maritime incidents, plus this new word war, happens just weeks before Teodoro hosts counterpart defense chiefs, including Chinese Defense Minister Admiral Dong Jun, in Cebu. The Philippines, by mid-November, concludes its Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) chairmanship with the bloc’s 49th Summit.

At the Summit, the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea will surely be taken up — and potentially the aspiration for it to conclude by 2026 or the end of Manila’s chairmanship. Signs indicate that a COC acceptable to the diverse bloc and China is far from reality.

The summit will also follow a rather tense time for domestic politics — in the weeks prior, Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team is expected to present their case before the impeachment court. Duterte has also been accused of having financial ties to China through her husband’s company.

Her claim is that her supposed political persecution, to include the China ties claim, is turning the Philippines into a “troublemaker” in the region. Beijing has called Manila a “troublemaker” in the past, too.

There are issues beyond the Philippines that ultimately affect the domestic situation — among them, an oil crisis exacerbated by Manila’s sole treaty-ally’s actions against Iran and on the critical waterway that’s the Strait of Hormuz.

It’s uncanny timing — diplomatic tensions between China and the Philippines rise just before Manila hosts a bloc with varying degrees of comfort and a wide range of approaches in handling a swashbuckling superpower neighbor like Beijing, and just as Marcos must oversee tense weeks in domestic politics.

Then there are issues way, way beyond Manila’s control. 2026 has seen the highest military expenditures across the world in history. We’re looking at the highest number of conflicts worldwide since the last world war. The United States is occupied by its war against Iran, and US President Donald Trump has seemed to truly put the brakes on their aid of Ukraine. The latter is a worrying point for Europe, which has in turn grown weary of its traditional ally, Washington.
As rhetoric between Manila and China escalates, one can only wonder what the only other world superpower is thinking. – Rappler.com
