articles.title: UK fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
articles.summary: The UK is sending military support to Saudi Arabia as Iran-aligned Houthi rebels launch repeated attacks on the kingdom.

image.caption: Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to fly missions to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks [FILE: November 21, 2024]Image: Joan Valls/Urbanandsport/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against increasing attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, the UK government announced on Tuesday.
The aircraft will protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from drones and missiles, the Ministry of Defense said. They will not carry out offensive strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable," British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said.
He particularly condemned attacks on Riyadh's international airport, which has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of October.

blocks.caption: Riyadh's international airport has seen a string of attacks claimed by the HouthisImage: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: Strikes on the airport have killed at least 18 people and wounded hundreds this month, according to reports.
What additional military support is Britain providing?
The deployment follows a request from Saudi Arabia and expands military assistance announced by London in September.

Britain will also send an Atlas A400M military transport aircraft and military advisers. It has extended its offer to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft operating against the Houthis for another 90 days.
The announcement comes as Yemen's civil war continues to escalate following the collapse of a years-long truce in September.

Houthi attacks have increasingly targeted Saudi oil facilities and civilian infrastructure. The rebels have also imposed a naval blockade and attacked tankers, disrupting oil exports and pushing up energy prices.

blocks.caption: Houthi rebels have targeted oil facilities in Saudi Arabia too [PHOTO: October 3]Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: Inside Yemen, authorities said a Houthi strike on Monday killed 58 people at a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces.
Saudi Arabia and the United States accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.
How is the conflict affecting Saudi Arabia's economy?
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, informally known as "Davos in the Desert," until 2027.
The event, originally scheduled for October 26-29, was expected to attract leading international financiers.
According to media reports, major banks and private equity firms had raised security concerns about attending the event.
The conference is a key part of Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy away from oil.

articles.title: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots
articles.summary: In France and beyond there is widespread disagreement over what led to some of the worst unrest seen in French cities in modern history.

blocks.text: "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"

Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped her and her friend to ask what they thought of what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."

But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.

French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.

French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.

A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections.

The mass looting of what's said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?

Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. President Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.

Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts has lead former French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.

Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's Interior minister Bernard Quintin, warned of the 'TikTokisation' of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liege on "known far left groups".

In France, Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu and his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire," said Nunez. On Tuesday Mr Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he'd accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.

Mélonchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.
What do the students say?

In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.
"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.

But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."
France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.
The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.

Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist Prime Minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."

Mélonchon went on to apparently imply Mr Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances."
France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.

As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's Interior Minister admitted there weren't enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance. Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.
Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration, National Rally Party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.

She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.
She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".
She ended her video by reminding French voters they'd have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in 6 months time.
Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed border message and, like US President Trump and Vice US President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday.
Teacher, Mar, complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services," she said.

"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."
But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".
That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.
These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives.
What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask?

Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.

According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. (The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.)

So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protestors, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.

Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?

articles.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
articles.summary:
Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda…

blocks.text: Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

blocks.caption: Health workers on the frontlines of the Ebola response receive vaccination in Beni, DRC.  Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters

blocks.text: Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
articles.summary: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look at a possible mega-merger.

blocks.text: Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.
While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.
Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading.
The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.
That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn.
SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year.
Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks.

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.
Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.
Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield".
He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.
While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.
SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.

articles.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
articles.summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
ByPaul Adams
Diplomatic correspondent

The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.

But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.

After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.

The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.

The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.

Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.

Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.

Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.

Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.

A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated

blocks.text: Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated

A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.

Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.

Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

articles.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary:
Police seized dozens of hepatitis B vaccines from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns

Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy…

blocks.text: Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.
Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.
“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.
The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

articles.title: ‘Bad decisions’: Man convicted for taking Peachy the flamingo from Las Vegas hotel
articles.summary:
Mitchell Fairbarn found guilty of animal cruelty after prosecutors say he hurt and frightened the 27-year-old bird

A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching…

blocks.text: A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges on Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconic Las Vegas hotel.
Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.

Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room on 3 March. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.
After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts against the Ontario, Canada, man.

Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for 1 December. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanor conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.
His lawyer also had no comment.

After the incident, the flamingo was mostly unharmed but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

Prosecutors told jurors earlier that Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor. Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway at the famous hotel. The Flamingo is one of the oldest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and its well-known flamingo habitat also features hummingbirds, turtles, koi and other species.
Peachy was missing some feathers after being taken.

Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported that someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.
Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fueled by drunkenness”, the defense attorney Tomsheck said. But he added that his client never intended any harm to the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck said. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”
Fairbarn could be seen in court at one point with head lowered, hands covering his eyes.

The man had received death threats after taking the flamingo, and he was unable to leave the US when his father died while Fairbarn was awaiting trial, said Haley Willming, the Clark county prosecutor. While those events were unfortunate, the prosecutor said, “none of that would have happened had he not done what he did, had he not made the choices he made”.
Jurors began deliberating shortly before midday after closing arguments on Monday morning.
Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.
“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff
articles.summary:
Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it

To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious…

blocks.text: To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.

But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.
Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.
Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.
John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokingly described himself as a “musician (and a hunk)”.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
The Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabet introduced himself to his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.
Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.
Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse, posted a photograph of herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.

Prominent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha, whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, who identified as a political scientist and astrophysicist.

All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.
Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.

“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.
“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.

Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also has well-documented ties to members of Rio’s mafia underworld and once employed the relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trump recently designated a foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonaro voiced surprise at those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.
On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.
Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.

The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.

Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwinger won the 4 October first round by more than 2m votes.

articles.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 200 people, sources say
articles.summary: A truck carrying people to a funeral and a market alleged to be supplying fuel to the RSF were targeted.
articles.byline: Richard Kagoe, Lucy Fleming, Richard Irvine-Brown

blocks.text: Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 200 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 73 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.

The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.
Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.
The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.

"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday, external.
The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.
Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.

The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) and had killed 73 people, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.
"We were surprised by bombing and thick smoke inside Amiet Common Market, which is located 10km [six miles] from Abyei town," he said.

BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.

It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market.
Ngor told the Reuters news agency that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.
Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town.

"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.
It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.
Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

articles.title: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
articles.summary:
Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices

A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the…

blocks.text: A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.
The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.

A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.

Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.

They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.

Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.
Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”

There is increasing recognition of the importance of Indigenous stewardship of the Amazon and other biomes that sequester carbon, shelter biodiversity and provide vital ecological services to the planet. But this role is increasingly difficult as Indigenous lands are threatened by miners, loggers, farmers and land grabbers, and as many of the young people of these often economically poor communities are exposed to the internet or lured away to wealthier cities.

How to sustain, encourage and reward Indigenous stewardship is a hot debate in the international aid and environmental community. Many previous payment schemes came with strings attached, such as the Brazilian government’s bolsa família, which has child education obligations, or bolsa verde, which has conservation activity requirements.

blocks.caption: Asháninka Indigenous people from Brazil and Peru dance and sing at dawn during an annual celebration. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP

blocks.text: The authors of the new study say the project – which was drawn up with local women’s groups – is the first to offer an unconditional basic income to an Indigenous community in the Amazon.

The lead author, Dr Neil Howard, said: “All of this helps ethical conservation. The incentive to exploit or abandon land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.”
after newsletter promotion
To boost the impact, the project delivered a voluntary “cash plus” complementary programme of community-led education on finance, conservation and climate change.

Other academics are more cautious about the environmental impacts of cash transfers, pointing out that similar studies elsewhere have found they can lead to an increase in deforestation as people use the extra cash to expand agriculture.

In some parts of the Amazon, cash payments are used to buy motorbikes and cars, which increases demand for more roads. There are also reports of Indigenous communities becoming more exposed to drugs when they visit cities to collect transfers.

The authors of the new report acknowledge that wider research is needed on the ecological impacts of unconditional basic income. Their two-year study was small, covering little over 500 hectares (1,235 acres) of forest. They did not measure changes in vegetation or soil quality, nor account for the influence of any separate projects that might have been affecting community behaviour.
Despite these limitations, they say the early results have excited the cash-for-conservation network of civil society organisations.

“Yes, this is an experimental pilot and and we could do with something much larger,” Howard said. “But this is very pioneering. My hope is that the trade-off between scale and innovation tips in this direction.”

articles.title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
articles.summary: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday

blocks.text: India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.

Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupeesvaluation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.

Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.

At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
after newsletter promotion

Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.

Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

articles.title: She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home
articles.summary:
​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism

Before 24 July, a person I will…

blocks.text: Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.

That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.

“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.

The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.

I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.

The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.

R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.

After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.

Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)
“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”

But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.

“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”

With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.
During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.

Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.
“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.
R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.

Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)

R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.
“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.
Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.

It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A still from award-winning film Selvi.

blocks.text: Culture | Two Indian films won awards at the Busan international film festival. Birds in the Dark by Shashank Walia was awarded the Songwon Vision audience prize and Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi won the HyLife Vision as well as the Taipei Film Commission award.
after newsletter promotion

Politics | The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, will land in Mumbai on 20 October for his second visit to India this year. Rubio will meet foreign minister S Jaishankar and then travel to Jamnagar, home to Reliance Industries’ massive refinery.

Imran Khan | Days after the Bollywood actor Imran Khan appeared at a Mumbai protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, authorities asked him to leave the country by 28 October over what they described as a violation of the Foreigners Act. The action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya against Khan, who is a US citizen.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Media Ka Loktantra by Vineet Kumar. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.

“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: The National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) plant in Dadri. Photograph: Prakash Singh/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 – were critically low on coal stocks (£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: A felt sculpture by Sagarika Sundaram at the Henry Moore Institute. Photograph: Rob Harris

blocks.text: Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.

“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.

The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Alberta voters reject plan for referendum to leave Canada, CBC projects
articles.summary:
Projection delivers a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward…

blocks.text: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected, delivering a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity.

With more than 1 million votes counted early Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation. About a third of ballots had been counted.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours – but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening, the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.
Prime minister Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government.
“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.
The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, has said publicly that she will vote to remain in Canada, but that she will not require elected members of her party to do the same.

Her tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months, Smith has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.

The referendum has also become a political liability for Smith’s party, which has seen popular support tumble in recent months, including the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold during a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, told the Guardian the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city” amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.
“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” said Farkas.

“And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together because no result will permanently put this to bed,” he added, “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

articles.title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
articles.summary:
Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation

Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to

blocks.text: Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.

A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.

Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.

Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.

Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.

Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.
Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.

“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington considers a genocide.

The former commander-in-chief has recently conducted several regional visits to rebuild bilateral ties with neighbours, after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) regional bloc barred him from its summits for not following an Asean-brokered ‌peace plan.
During his most recent trip to Malaysia this month, the leader was given an official welcome and honour guard. Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.

blocks.caption: Aung San Suu Kyi pictured delivering a speech in 2020.  Photograph: Aung Shine Oo/AP

blocks.text: Phil Robertson, director at the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) group, said the Suu Kyi book photo op was part of Myanmar’s “quest for global legitimacy”.

“The bottom line is Asean has grown tired of arguing with Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s intransigent military leaders and having nothing to show for it, and they desperately want to move the bloc on to other, more cheery issues,” he said.

“So as the Asean dominoes fall to the Myanmar charm offensive, they just want to make their regional capitulation look good – and that requires Myanmar to play its part by trotting out Suu Kyi at occasional intervals to receive their latest beneficence.”
Min Aung Hlaing has also made efforts to reach out to Donald Trump’s administration, saying in a September interview with Time magazine that “it would be ideal if the US could cooperate with us”.

Weeks later, Reuters reported that the US and Myanmar officials had held talks in Naypyidaw and Tokyo, in part to shut down scam centres that target Americans, but which could be broadened to exploitation of Myanmar’s mineral deposits.

The US state department has said it is re-examining “the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country”. China has become Myanmar’s key global partner.

Myanmar has always denied the accusations of genocide, and Suu Kyi, who held the role of state counsellor at the time of the atrocities, defended the country at the international court of justice, disappointing many in her global support base.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
articles.summary: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday

blocks.text: More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.

Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.
The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.

It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.

“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”
The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.
Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

articles.title: Clean up begins after French riots but police remain
articles.summary: Outside of Paris, Marseille saw some of the worst damage, with shop owners reporting more than 600 premises having been looted.

blocks.text: Following a weekend of intense rioting across France, a clean up operation has begun - but tensions remain, with police still in position and a curfew in place in some big cities.
Outside of Paris, Marseille saw some of the worst damage, with shop owners reporting more than 600 premises having been looted.
From the port city in southern France, the BBC's Nick Beake explains some of the factors behind the protests.

articles.title: Ukraine says it carried out first drone airlift of wounded soldier from front line
articles.summary: The serviceman was surrounded by landmines and enemy drones so a ground rescue was not possible, Ukraine's military says.

blocks.text: The Ukrainian military has released footage of what it says is the world's first drone airlift of a wounded soldier from the front line.
The 92nd Assault Brigade said a ground rescue mission was not possible as the wounded serviceman was surrounded by landmines and there was high Russian drone activity in the area.
It says a "heavy" hexacopter, piloted by a remote operator, was able to maintain stability during the "very difficult" operation.
BBC Verify has found confirmed the identity of the army personnel involved in the video, and found no signs of AI generation of manipulation.
